payload.title: Rhetorical Analysis: A Night Nurse on the Discipline of Attention
payload.set_intro:
ALTON original passage
Commencement Address to the Dunmore Valley School of Nursing
Marisol Quenneville, charge nurse, Harrowgate Memorial Hospital night shift; commencement address delivered to the graduating class of the Dunmore Valley School of Nursing, 2019

¶1 (1) I have worked nights for nineteen years, and I will tell you the first thing the dark teaches: a hospital at three in the morning is never silent. (2) The monitors tick, the ice machine groans, somebody's call light blinks at the end of the hall like a slow pulse. (3) Most of that noise means nothing. (4) Some of it means everything. (5) The whole of our profession, I have come to believe, lives in the space between those two sentences.

¶2 (6) You have spent four years learning what to do. (7) You can run a line, titrate a drip, read a rhythm strip from across the room. (8) I am not here to add to that list. (9) I am here to talk about something that cannot be put on an exam: the discipline of paying attention. (10) I call it a discipline on purpose. (11) Attention is not a mood you fall into when the floor is quiet; it is a practice, like scrubbing in, that you perform the same way whether you feel like it or not.

¶3 (12) Let me tell you about a man in room 412. (13) This was my third year, and he was what we called a quiet patient, which is a dangerous compliment. (14) His vitals were fine. (15) His chart was fine. (16) He asked me, at twenty past two, whether I could open the blinds, and I nearly told him there was nothing out there but a parking lot. (17) Instead I asked him why. (18) He said he wanted to be able to see the sky in case he did not get another chance. (19) Nothing on the monitor had changed. (20) I called the resident anyway, and forty minutes later that man was in the cardiac unit, and he is, as far as I know, still alive, still looking at skies. (21) I did not save him with a skill. (22) I saved him by hearing a sentence.

¶4 (23) Now, I know what some of you are thinking, because I thought it too at your age. (24) You will have six patients, sometimes eight. (25) You will have a charting system that wants fourteen clicks to record a glass of water. (26) You will be tired in a way that has no name yet. (27) All of that is true, and I will not insult you by pretending otherwise. (28) But I have noticed, over nineteen years, that the nurses who miss things are not usually the busiest ones. (29) They are the ones who decided, somewhere along the way, that they already knew what they would find. (30) Fatigue takes your legs; certainty takes your eyes. (31) Of the two, certainty is the thief I fear.

¶5 (32) Our own quality committee at Harrowgate pulled the numbers last spring. (33) Of the seventy-one rapid-response calls on our medical floors last year, forty-four were triggered not by an alarm but by a nurse who simply reported that something was off. (34) Forty-four. (35) The machines, with all their sensors and their price tags, caught fewer than the people who were paying attention. (36) I do not say this to disparage the machines; they are good at what they measure. (37) I say it because what they do not measure is the thing you are being hired to notice.

¶6 (38) So here is what I ask of you, and it is small, and it is enormous. (39) When you walk into a room, stand still for three seconds before you touch anything. (40) Look at the hands, look at the breathing, look at what the patient is looking at. (41) Ask the second question. (42) The first question gets you a chart; the second gets you a person. (43) You will not do this perfectly. (44) I do not do it perfectly, and I have had nineteen years of practice. (45) But do it on purpose, every shift, until it stops being something you do and becomes something you are. (46) The hall will be loud tonight and every night after. (47) Listen anyway. (48) Congratulations, and welcome to the work.

parts.label: A
parts.prompt:
Speaker: Marisol Quenneville, a charge nurse who has worked the overnight shift at the fictional Harrowgate Memorial Hospital for nineteen years. Audience: the graduating class of the fictional Dunmore Valley School of Nursing, their families, and faculty. Occasion: a commencement ceremony; the graduates have finished their technical training and are about to begin work on busy hospital floors, and Quenneville has been invited to give the address.

The passage below is a commencement address delivered in 2019 by Marisol Quenneville, a night-shift charge nurse at Harrowgate Memorial Hospital, to the graduating class of the Dunmore Valley School of Nursing. Read the passage carefully. Write an essay that analyzes the rhetorical choices Quenneville makes to convince the new graduates that paying attention is a discipline they must practice deliberately.

Your essay should:
- Respond to the prompt with a thesis that presents a defensible analysis of the rhetorical choices Quenneville makes.
- Select and use evidence from the passage to support your line of reasoning.
- Explain how the evidence supports your line of reasoning by showing how specific choices advance Quenneville's purpose for this audience and occasion.
parts.model_answer:
Most graduation speakers tell the audience they are ready. Marisol Quenneville, a night-shift charge nurse speaking to new nurses, has a harder job: she has to respect the four years of skills they just earned while telling them those skills are not what will matter most at three in the morning. She handles this by moving the graduates from a scene, to a story, to a statistic, and finally to a direct charge, and at each step she narrows what "attention" means until it is no longer a feeling but a habit they can perform. Most importantly, she concedes the exhaustion waiting for them so she can move the real danger somewhere they did not expect, from fatigue to certainty.

Quenneville opens with a sound instead of advice. The monitors "tick," the ice machine "groans," and a call light blinks "like a slow pulse." For an audience that has only done clinicals, this puts them on the floor before she asks anything of them, and the simile is telling, because even the background noise is given a heartbeat. Then she splits it: "Most of that noise means nothing. Some of it means everything." Those two short sentences set up the problem the whole speech tries to solve, which is how to tell the difference. Only after that does she define her term, calling attention "a practice, like scrubbing in." This comparison is chosen for nurses specifically. Scrubbing in is something they have done hundreds of times no matter their mood, so she borrows a habit they already respect and attaches attention to it.

The story of the man in room 412 then shows what this practice looks like. Quenneville uses flat, repeated sentences, "His vitals were fine. His chart was fine," that sound like the reassuring data a tired nurse would accept. The repetition makes the twist hit harder: the only warning sign was a request to see the sky. She also admits she "nearly told him there was nothing out there but a parking lot," which matters because she isn't posing as a hero with perfect instincts. She was a third-year nurse, not far from where the graduates are now. Her conclusion, "I did not save him with a skill. I saved him by hearing a sentence," answers her own second paragraph: skills are what they learned in school, but hearing is what she is asking for now.

She knows the graduates will push back, so she lists their objections for them. The "fourteen clicks to record a glass of water" is specific enough to be funny, and it shows she hasn't forgotten what the job is like. Because she promises "I will not insult you by pretending otherwise," her rebuttal lands harder: the nurses who miss things "decided, somewhere along the way, that they already knew what they would find." The line "Fatigue takes your legs; certainty takes your eyes" makes this memorable, but it is also a little uncomfortable for people who were just tested on knowing the answers. The confidence school rewarded is the "thief." Her hospital data backs this up, with forty-four of seventy-one rapid-response calls coming from a nurse who noticed "something was off," and repeating "Forty-four" alone forces the audience to sit with it. Still, she adds that machines "are good at what they measure." She is not telling them to ignore monitors, which would sound reckless with faculty in the room; she is telling them their job starts where the measuring stops.

By the last paragraph she has earned the right to give orders, and the tone shifts to imperatives: "stand still for three seconds," "Ask the second question." The request is concrete enough to try on a first shift. Her admission "I do not do it perfectly" keeps it from sounding like a lecture, and it actually supports her definition, since a discipline is something you never finish practicing. The ending brings back the opening scene: "The hall will be loud tonight and every night after. Listen anyway." The noise from the first paragraph hasn't gone away, and she doesn't pretend it will. Two words are the last instruction she leaves them with, which is about the right length for something to remember at three in the morning.

rubric_rows.criterion: Thesis must make an analytical claim about the relationship between at least one choice and the purpose (convincing new nurses that attention is a deliberate discipline). A thesis that argues Quenneville is 'effective' with no indication of how is not sufficient. A thesis that names devices but also asserts what they accomplish for this audience earns the point. Listing device names with only a generic purpose ('to convince them') does not earn the point; the claim must say what the choices do for these listeners.

Choices that count include: the opening sensory description and simile (sentences 1 to 2); the antithesis 'Most of that noise means nothing. Some of it means everything' (3 to 4); the definition of attention as a discipline and the scrubbing-in simile (9 to 11); the room 412 anecdote with its short parallel sentences (12 to 22); the concession to workload and fatigue followed by the rebuttal that certainty, not busyness, causes misses (23 to 29); the metaphors 'Fatigue takes your legs; certainty takes your eyes' and 'certainty is the thief' (30 to 31); the hospital statistic and the one-word sentence 'Forty-four' (32 to 35); the qualification about machines (36 to 37); the shift to direct imperative instructions and a warmer tone (38 to 48); the two-word sentence 'Listen anyway' (47), which comes just before the closing congratulations. Student commentary should connect choices to the specific audience: new graduates proud of technical skill who are about to be overwhelmed. Device labels are not required if the student describes the choice accurately.

Do not award for merely using sophisticated vocabulary, for a long introduction about nursing in general, or for a single clever sentence in the conclusion. The point is for thinking carried through the essay.

Scoring guide (ALTON practice rubric, not official College Board scoring). Each essay is worth 6 points.
Thesis (0-1): Thesis must make an analytical claim about the relationship between at least one choice and the purpose (convincing new nurses that attention is a deliberate discipline). A thesis that argues Quenneville is 'effective' with no indication of how is not sufficient. A thesis that names devices but also asserts what they accomplish for this audience earns the point. Listing device names with only a generic purpose ('to convince them') does not earn the point; the claim must say what the choices do for these listeners.
   - 1: A defensible claim about how Quenneville's choices advance her purpose, stated in the introduction or elsewhere. Acceptable examples: she builds credibility through nineteen years of night-shift experience and then uses a single patient's story to redefine attention as a skill rather than a feeling; she anticipates the graduates' exhaustion so she can relocate the real danger from fatigue to certainty; she pairs a hospital statistic with an anecdote to show that human noticing outperforms machines. The thesis may be a single sentence and need not preview every device.
   - 0: No thesis, or a thesis that only restates the prompt (for example, 'Quenneville uses many rhetorical choices to convince the graduates to pay attention'), or a thesis that merely summarizes the speech's content or lists devices without any claim about how they work.
Evidence and Commentary (0-4): Choices that count include: the opening sensory description and simile (sentences 1 to 2); the antithesis 'Most of that noise means nothing. Some of it means everything' (3 to 4); the definition of attention as a discipline and the scrubbing-in simile (9 to 11); the room 412 anecdote with its short parallel sentences (12 to 22); the concession to workload and fatigue followed by the rebuttal that certainty, not busyness, causes misses (23 to 29); the metaphors 'Fatigue takes your legs; certainty takes your eyes' and 'certainty is the thief' (30 to 31); the hospital statistic and the one-word sentence 'Forty-four' (32 to 35); the qualification about machines (36 to 37); the shift to direct imperative instructions and a warmer tone (38 to 48); the two-word sentence 'Listen anyway' (47), which comes just before the closing congratulations. Student commentary should connect choices to the specific audience: new graduates proud of technical skill who are about to be overwhelmed. Device labels are not required if the student describes the choice accurately.
   - 4: Consistently specific evidence drawn from across the speech and commentary that explains how each selected choice advances the purpose for this audience and occasion. The essay accounts for the speech as a developing whole (for example, how the opening sensory scene sets up the later contrast between noise that means nothing and noise that means everything, or how the concession in paragraph 4 earns the authority of the closing instructions). Explanations are precise about what the audience is asked to believe or do and why the choice makes that more likely.
   - 3: Uses specific evidence from at least two or three different parts of the speech and explains for most of it how the choice works on this audience of graduating nurses. Commentary may occasionally lapse into summary or overstate (for example, claiming the statistic 'proves' machines are useless), but a line of reasoning is sustained.
   - 2: Quotes or references specific moments but commentary is thin or repetitive: identifies that sentence 30 is a metaphor or that paragraph 4 is a concession but explains the effect in a generic way ('this helps her argument') or only once in the essay. Line of reasoning is present but underdeveloped or inconsistent.
   - 1: Mostly summarizes or paraphrases the speech (for example, retells the story of room 412) with general statements such as 'this makes the audience feel emotion' and no explanation tied to purpose. May name devices without quoting or locating them.
   - 0: Simply restates the thesis, repeats the prompt, or offers evidence unrelated to the passage.
Sophistication (0-1): Do not award for merely using sophisticated vocabulary, for a long introduction about nursing in general, or for a single clever sentence in the conclusion. The point is for thinking carried through the essay.
   - 1: Earns the point by doing at least one of the following consistently: explaining how Quenneville's choices respond to the specific rhetorical situation (a commencement where she must honor the graduates' training while telling them it is not enough); tracing a tension in the speech such as her respect for and limitation of monitors, or her admission in 44 that she herself fails; showing how the speech's structure moves the audience from scene to story to data to charge; or writing with a controlled, precise style that itself demonstrates careful attention to the text.
   - 0: Commentary stays at the level of identifying and explaining individual choices; prose may be clear but does not explore tensions, complexities, or the rhetorical situation in depth. Also 0 if the essay's style is inflated or vague in ways that obscure the analysis.
Note: Score the three rows independently; an essay may earn Row B points without a thesis point.
Note: Evidence may be quoted or closely paraphrased with sentence references; exact device terminology is not required if the choice is accurately described.
Note: Do not reward device-spotting lists. Three devices explained well outweigh eight devices named.
Note: Commentary that explains effect on the specific audience (new nurses, proud of skills, about to face understaffed floors) should be rated higher than commentary about 'the reader' in general.
Note: An essay that argues the speech is partly unpersuasive is acceptable if it still analyzes how the choices are meant to work.
Note: Misreadings that reverse meaning (for example, claiming Quenneville says machines should be ignored) weaken Row B but do not zero it if other evidence is sound.

   - "she concedes the exhaustion waiting for them so she can move the real danger somewhere they did not expect, from fatigue to certainty" - Defensible thesis that ties a specific choice (the concession) to its job for this audience. It goes past 'she is effective' and says how the move works. Earns the point.
   - "at each step she narrows what "attention" means until it is no longer a feeling but a habit they can perform" - Sets up a line of reasoning (scene, story, statistic, charge) that connects directly to the purpose of redefining attention as a discipline.

Sample response, middle score (4/6; Thesis 1, Evidence and commentary 3, Sophistication 0):
In her commencement address, Marisol Quenneville wants the new nurses to see attention as a discipline and not a feeling, and she does this by using her own long experience to build trust and then using a story and a statistic to show that noticing people matters more than relying on machines. Because the graduates are proud of their technical skills, she has to convince them without insulting what they have learned.

She starts by describing the hospital at three in the morning, where "the monitors tick, the ice machine groans, somebody's call light blinks at the end of the hall like a slow pulse." This sensory detail puts the graduates in the place they are about to work, and the simile of the call light as a pulse makes the hospital seem alive. Then she says "Most of that noise means nothing. Some of it means everything." The short sentences set up the problem the rest of the speech is about, which is telling the difference. This is a good way to start because the graduates have never worked a night shift and she is showing them what it is like.

The most memorable part is the story of the man in room 412. Quenneville says his vitals were fine and his chart was fine, and then he asks her to open the blinds. The short sentences like "His vitals were fine. His chart was fine." sound calm and routine, which makes the moment when she asks "why" stand out. She ends with "I did not save him with a skill. I saved him by hearing a sentence." This is aimed right at the graduates, who just spent four years learning skills, and she is telling them that skill is not the whole job. The story makes her argument feel real instead of just an opinion.

Quenneville also admits the problems the graduates will face. She says they will have "six patients, sometimes eight" and be tired "in a way that has no name yet." By saying "I will not insult you by pretending otherwise" she shows she is being honest, so the audience is more likely to listen. Then she says "Fatigue takes your legs; certainty takes your eyes," which moves the danger from being busy to being sure of yourself. The metaphor of certainty as a thief makes it sound like something the graduates should be afraid of.

Next she uses the statistic that forty-four of seventy-one rapid-response calls came from nurses and not alarms. The one-word sentence "Forty-four" gives it emphasis. This proves that people notice things that machines do not, though she is careful to say she does not "disparage the machines."

At the end her tone changes to direct commands like "stand still for three seconds" and "Ask the second question." These are small, so the graduates can actually do them. She admits "I do not do it perfectly," which makes her seem human. Her last instruction, "Listen anyway," is short and tells them to keep paying attention even when the hall is loud. Overall, Quenneville uses story, honesty, and evidence to persuade the graduates that attention is something they have to choose to practice.
   - "she does this by using her own long experience to build trust and then using a story and a statistic to show that noticing people matters more than relying on machines" - Defensible claim about how choices (credibility, anecdote, statistic) advance the purpose for this audience. Earns the thesis point, though 'matters more than' slightly overstates her stance on machines.
   - "This sensory detail puts the graduates in the place they are about to work, and the simile of the call light as a pulse makes the hospital seem alive." - Specific quotation with some link to the audience, but the effect ('seems alive') is general and not tied to the discipline argument.
   - "The short sentences like "His vitals were fine. His chart was fine." sound calm and routine, which makes the moment when she asks "why" stand out." - Good, specific observation about parallel short sentences and contrast; this is the strongest commentary in the essay and links to the graduates' skill-focused training.
   - "The story makes her argument feel real instead of just an opinion." - Generic commentary ('feel real') that could apply to any anecdote; does not explain how it moves nurses toward practicing attention.
   - "This proves that people notice things that machines do not, though she is careful to say she does not "disparage the machines."" - Overstates with 'proves' and the explanation is brief; does not explore why the one-word 'Forty-four' works on this audience or the tension with trusting monitors.
   - "Overall, Quenneville uses story, honesty, and evidence to persuade the graduates that attention is something they have to choose to practice." - Conclusion restates the thesis. The essay moves through the speech in order but mostly explains devices one at a time and does not develop the commencement situation or tensions, so no sophistication point.

Sample response, low score (2/6; Thesis 0, Evidence and commentary 2, Sophistication 0):
Marisol Quenneville gives a speech to the graduating nurses about paying attention. She uses many rhetorical choices like stories, statistics, and metaphors to convince them that attention is something they have to practice. This essay will show how she does this.

In the beginning she talks about the hospital at three in the morning and says the monitors tick and the ice machine groans. This gives the audience a picture of what working nights is like. She also says that she has worked nights for nineteen years, so she has a lot of experience and the graduates will listen to her.

Next she tells a story about a man in room 412. He asked her to open the blinds because he wanted to see the sky in case he did not get another chance. She called the resident and the man ended up in the cardiac unit and he was still alive. This story is very emotional and it makes the audience feel that noticing is important. It shows that she saved him by hearing a sentence and not with a skill.

Then she says that the graduates will be tired and have six or eight patients. She says "Fatigue takes your legs; certainty takes your eyes." This is a metaphor and it helps her argument because it shows that being certain is bad. She also calls certainty a thief.

She also uses a statistic that forty-four out of seventy-one rapid response calls came from nurses and not alarms. She says "Forty-four" by itself which makes it stand out. This shows that nurses are better than machines at noticing things.

At the end she tells them what to do, like stand still for three seconds and ask the second question. She ends her instructions with "Listen anyway." This is a good ending because it is short and the audience remembers it.

In conclusion, Quenneville uses a story, a metaphor, and a statistic to persuade the graduates that attention is a discipline. Her speech is effective because it uses these choices well.
   - "She uses many rhetorical choices like stories, statistics, and metaphors to convince them that attention is something they have to practice." - This restates the prompt and lists devices without claiming how they work for this audience. It earns no thesis point.
   - "Her speech is effective because it uses these choices well." - The conclusion only says the speech is 'effective' with no indication of how, which the rubric says is not sufficient for the thesis point.
   - "This gives the audience a picture of what working nights is like." - The commentary is generic. It does not connect the sensory opening to the later noise-that-means-nothing versus noise-that-means-everything contrast or to the graduates' situation.
   - "This story is very emotional and it makes the audience feel that noticing is important." - This is mostly summary of room 412 plus a vague 'makes the audience feel' statement. It does not explain the short parallel sentences or the shift from skill to hearing, or tie them to proud, skill-focused graduates.
   - "This is a metaphor and it helps her argument because it shows that being certain is bad." - The metaphor is identified and quoted, but the effect is generic ('helps her argument'). The essay ignores the concession in paragraph 4 and how it moves the danger from fatigue to certainty for tired new nurses.
   - "This shows that nurses are better than machines at noticing things." - This is a relevant moment, and 'Forty-four' is noted, but the commentary overstates the point and skips her qualification about machines (sentences 36-37). It never explains why data persuades this audience.
   - "This is a good ending because it is short and the audience remembers it." - This is a thin, generic explanation. It does not address the shift to imperatives or the warmer tone.
   - "In conclusion, Quenneville uses a story, a metaphor, and a statistic to persuade the graduates that attention is a discipline." - The essay treats the devices one at a time and repeats the prompt. It does not engage the commencement situation or the speech's movement from scene to story to data to charge, so it earns no sophistication point.

el_frq.title: Rhetorical Analysis: A Night Nurse on the Discipline of Attention

prompt.scenario: Speaker: Marisol Quenneville, a charge nurse who has worked the overnight shift at the fictional Harrowgate Memorial Hospital for nineteen years. Audience: the graduating class of the fictional Dunmore Valley School of Nursing, their families, and faculty. Occasion: a commencement ceremony; the graduates have finished their technical training and are about to begin work on busy hospital floors, and Quenneville has been invited to give the address.
prompt.task: The passage below is a commencement address delivered in 2019 by Marisol Quenneville, a night-shift charge nurse at Harrowgate Memorial Hospital, to the graduating class of the Dunmore Valley School of Nursing. Read the passage carefully. Write an essay that analyzes the rhetorical choices Quenneville makes to convince the new graduates that paying attention is a discipline they must practice deliberately.
requirements: Respond to the prompt with a thesis that presents a defensible analysis of the rhetorical choices Quenneville makes.
Select and use evidence from the passage to support your line of reasoning.
Explain how the evidence supports your line of reasoning by showing how specific choices advance Quenneville's purpose for this audience and occasion.

sources.title: Commencement Address to the Dunmore Valley School of Nursing
sources.attribution: Marisol Quenneville, charge nurse, Harrowgate Memorial Hospital night shift; commencement address delivered to the graduating class of the Dunmore Valley School of Nursing, 2019
paragraphs: (1) I have worked nights for nineteen years, and I will tell you the first thing the dark teaches: a hospital at three in the morning is never silent.
(2) The monitors tick, the ice machine groans, somebody's call light blinks at the end of the hall like a slow pulse.
(3) Most of that noise means nothing.
(4) Some of it means everything.
(5) The whole of our profession, I have come to believe, lives in the space between those two sentences.
(6) You have spent four years learning what to do.
(7) You can run a line, titrate a drip, read a rhythm strip from across the room.
(8) I am not here to add to that list.
(9) I am here to talk about something that cannot be put on an exam: the discipline of paying attention.
(10) I call it a discipline on purpose.
(11) Attention is not a mood you fall into when the floor is quiet; it is a practice, like scrubbing in, that you perform the same way whether you feel like it or not.
(12) Let me tell you about a man in room 412.
(13) This was my third year, and he was what we called a quiet patient, which is a dangerous compliment.
(14) His vitals were fine.
(15) His chart was fine.
(16) He asked me, at twenty past two, whether I could open the blinds, and I nearly told him there was nothing out there but a parking lot.
(17) Instead I asked him why.
(18) He said he wanted to be able to see the sky in case he did not get another chance.
(19) Nothing on the monitor had changed.
(20) I called the resident anyway, and forty minutes later that man was in the cardiac unit, and he is, as far as I know, still alive, still looking at skies.
(21) I did not save him with a skill.
(22) I saved him by hearing a sentence.
(23) Now, I know what some of you are thinking, because I thought it too at your age.
(24) You will have six patients, sometimes eight.
(25) You will have a charting system that wants fourteen clicks to record a glass of water.
(26) You will be tired in a way that has no name yet.
(27) All of that is true, and I will not insult you by pretending otherwise.
(28) But I have noticed, over nineteen years, that the nurses who miss things are not usually the busiest ones.
(29) They are the ones who decided, somewhere along the way, that they already knew what they would find.
(30) Fatigue takes your legs; certainty takes your eyes.
(31) Of the two, certainty is the thief I fear.
(32) Our own quality committee at Harrowgate pulled the numbers last spring.
(33) Of the seventy-one rapid-response calls on our medical floors last year, forty-four were triggered not by an alarm but by a nurse who simply reported that something was off.
(34) Forty-four.
(35) The machines, with all their sensors and their price tags, caught fewer than the people who were paying attention.
(36) I do not say this to disparage the machines; they are good at what they measure.
(37) I say it because what they do not measure is the thing you are being hired to notice.
(38) So here is what I ask of you, and it is small, and it is enormous.
(39) When you walk into a room, stand still for three seconds before you touch anything.
(40) Look at the hands, look at the breathing, look at what the patient is looking at.
(41) Ask the second question.
(42) The first question gets you a chart; the second gets you a person.
(43) You will not do this perfectly.
(44) I do not do it perfectly, and I have had nineteen years of practice.
(45) But do it on purpose, every shift, until it stops being something you do and becomes something you are.
(46) The hall will be loud tonight and every night after.
(47) Listen anyway.
(48) Congratulations, and welcome to the work.
sources.stance: Attention is a practiced discipline, not a mood, and it is the core of nursing.

rows.name: Thesis

descriptors.0: No thesis, or a thesis that only restates the prompt (for example, 'Quenneville uses many rhetorical choices to convince the graduates to pay attention'), or a thesis that merely summarizes the speech's content or lists devices without any claim about how they work.
descriptors.1: A defensible claim about how Quenneville's choices advance her purpose, stated in the introduction or elsewhere. Acceptable examples: she builds credibility through nineteen years of night-shift experience and then uses a single patient's story to redefine attention as a skill rather than a feeling; she anticipates the graduates' exhaustion so she can relocate the real danger from fatigue to certainty; she pairs a hospital statistic with an anecdote to show that human noticing outperforms machines. The thesis may be a single sentence and need not preview every device.

rows.task_specific: Thesis must make an analytical claim about the relationship between at least one choice and the purpose (convincing new nurses that attention is a deliberate discipline). A thesis that argues Quenneville is 'effective' with no indication of how is not sufficient. A thesis that names devices but also asserts what they accomplish for this audience earns the point. Listing device names with only a generic purpose ('to convince them') does not earn the point; the claim must say what the choices do for these listeners.

rows.name: Evidence and Commentary

descriptors.0: Simply restates the thesis, repeats the prompt, or offers evidence unrelated to the passage.
descriptors.1: Mostly summarizes or paraphrases the speech (for example, retells the story of room 412) with general statements such as 'this makes the audience feel emotion' and no explanation tied to purpose. May name devices without quoting or locating them.
descriptors.2: Quotes or references specific moments but commentary is thin or repetitive: identifies that sentence 30 is a metaphor or that paragraph 4 is a concession but explains the effect in a generic way ('this helps her argument') or only once in the essay. Line of reasoning is present but underdeveloped or inconsistent.
descriptors.3: Uses specific evidence from at least two or three different parts of the speech and explains for most of it how the choice works on this audience of graduating nurses. Commentary may occasionally lapse into summary or overstate (for example, claiming the statistic 'proves' machines are useless), but a line of reasoning is sustained.
descriptors.4: Consistently specific evidence drawn from across the speech and commentary that explains how each selected choice advances the purpose for this audience and occasion. The essay accounts for the speech as a developing whole (for example, how the opening sensory scene sets up the later contrast between noise that means nothing and noise that means everything, or how the concession in paragraph 4 earns the authority of the closing instructions). Explanations are precise about what the audience is asked to believe or do and why the choice makes that more likely.

rows.task_specific: Choices that count include: the opening sensory description and simile (sentences 1 to 2); the antithesis 'Most of that noise means nothing. Some of it means everything' (3 to 4); the definition of attention as a discipline and the scrubbing-in simile (9 to 11); the room 412 anecdote with its short parallel sentences (12 to 22); the concession to workload and fatigue followed by the rebuttal that certainty, not busyness, causes misses (23 to 29); the metaphors 'Fatigue takes your legs; certainty takes your eyes' and 'certainty is the thief' (30 to 31); the hospital statistic and the one-word sentence 'Forty-four' (32 to 35); the qualification about machines (36 to 37); the shift to direct imperative instructions and a warmer tone (38 to 48); the two-word sentence 'Listen anyway' (47), which comes just before the closing congratulations. Student commentary should connect choices to the specific audience: new graduates proud of technical skill who are about to be overwhelmed. Device labels are not required if the student describes the choice accurately.

rows.name: Sophistication

descriptors.0: Commentary stays at the level of identifying and explaining individual choices; prose may be clear but does not explore tensions, complexities, or the rhetorical situation in depth. Also 0 if the essay's style is inflated or vague in ways that obscure the analysis.
descriptors.1: Earns the point by doing at least one of the following consistently: explaining how Quenneville's choices respond to the specific rhetorical situation (a commencement where she must honor the graduates' training while telling them it is not enough); tracing a tension in the speech such as her respect for and limitation of monitors, or her admission in 44 that she herself fails; showing how the speech's structure moves the audience from scene to story to data to charge; or writing with a controlled, precise style that itself demonstrates careful attention to the text.

rows.task_specific: Do not award for merely using sophisticated vocabulary, for a long introduction about nursing in general, or for a single clever sentence in the conclusion. The point is for thinking carried through the essay.

scoring_notes: Score the three rows independently; an essay may earn Row B points without a thesis point.
Evidence may be quoted or closely paraphrased with sentence references; exact device terminology is not required if the choice is accurately described.
Do not reward device-spotting lists. Three devices explained well outweigh eight devices named.
Commentary that explains effect on the specific audience (new nurses, proud of skills, about to face understaffed floors) should be rated higher than commentary about 'the reader' in general.
An essay that argues the speech is partly unpersuasive is acceptable if it still analyzes how the choices are meant to work.
Misreadings that reverse meaning (for example, claiming Quenneville says machines should be ignored) weaken Row B but do not zero it if other evidence is sound.

defensible_positions: Quenneville establishes authority through specific night-shift detail, then uses a patient's story to redefine attention as a trained practice rather than a feeling, so that the graduates accept her closing instructions as professional technique.

By conceding the graduates' coming exhaustion and then naming certainty rather than fatigue as the real threat, Quenneville removes the audience's strongest excuse and makes attention a matter of choice.
The speech pairs human-scale evidence (one sentence from one patient) with institutional data (forty-four of seventy-one calls) to argue that noticing is both measurable and irreplaceable.
The structure moves from sensory scene to story to statistic to command, so that the final imperatives feel earned rather than preached.
lines_of_reasoning: Ethos first (nineteen years, three in the morning, the ice machine), then anecdote that turns a skill-proud audience toward listening, then concession that pre-empts objections, then a charge delivered in short imperatives.
Track the contrast between measurement and noticing: monitor unchanged in 19, machines in 35 to 37, chart versus person in 42.
Track sentence length: long descriptive sentences in paragraph 1 narrow to four-word sentences in 14 and 15, the one-word 34, and the two-word 47, each compressing emphasis at a turning point.

rhetorical_choices.effect: Specific night-shift details (nineteen years, three in the morning, the ice machine) establish that she speaks from the floor, not the lectern, so graduates will trust her over textbook advice.
The call light blinking 'like a slow pulse' turns the hospital itself into a body to be monitored, foreshadowing the claim that attention is the nurse's real instrument.
Two balanced short sentences frame the whole speech as the problem of telling meaningless noise from meaningful noise, which is exactly what attention does.
Defining attention as a discipline, with the scrubbing-in comparison, moves it from a personality trait to a procedure the audience already respects and performs.
Acknowledging the graduates' skills before withholding more of them honors their training while opening space for something it did not cover.
The room 412 story gives a concrete case where the monitor was wrong and a sentence was right, making the abstract claim about attention vivid and memorable.
'His vitals were fine. His chart were fine' in flat parallel form mimics the false reassurance of routine data before the turn.
The patient's wish to see the sky 'in case he did not get another chance' creates emotional stakes that no chart captures, moving graduates to want to be the nurse who asks why.
She grants workload and exhaustion in full, then shifts blame for missed signs to certainty, disarming the excuse before the audience can raise it.
'Fatigue takes your legs; certainty takes your eyes' and 'certainty is the thief' make a mental habit into a physical loss and a criminal, intensifying the warning.
Forty-four of seventy-one calls supplies institutional, countable proof that human noticing is not sentimental but measurable, appealing to graduates trained on data.
The one-word sentence 'Forty-four' after a long clause forces the number to land as a spoken beat.
Refusing to disparage machines keeps her credible with technically trained listeners and sharpens the claim to what machines cannot measure.
The move from reflective storytelling to direct imperatives ('stand still,' 'look,' 'ask') converts the argument into an actionable practice at the moment of commencement.
'The first question gets you a chart; the second gets you a person' compresses the whole argument into a memorable rule.
Returning to 'nineteen years' at the end, now paired with her own imperfection, humanizes the authority established at the start and makes the charge humble rather than preachy.
The two-word 'Listen anyway' after the noisy hall sentence enacts the discipline it names: a brief, deliberate act of attention amid noise.

source_uses.usable_for: All evidence; students should cite by sentence number or quotation.

common_pitfalls: Retelling the room 412 story as plot summary instead of analyzing why it is placed after the definition of attention and told in short, flat sentences.
Claiming the statistic in sentence 33 proves machines are useless, ignoring the qualification in sentences 36 to 37.
Listing devices (metaphor, anecdote, repetition) with one sentence each and no connection to the graduates as an audience.
Treating pathos as 'making the audience sad' rather than explaining how the patient's wish to see the sky dramatizes what a monitor cannot measure.
Ignoring the concession in paragraph 4 or describing it as weakening the argument rather than as a move that lets her relocate the danger from fatigue to certainty.
Missing the tone shift in the final paragraph from reflective storytelling to direct imperatives.
Writing a thesis that says only that the speech is 'effective' or 'uses ethos, pathos, and logos.'

samples.essay:
Most graduation speakers tell the audience they are ready. Marisol Quenneville, a night-shift charge nurse speaking to new nurses, has a harder job: she has to respect the four years of skills they just earned while telling them those skills are not what will matter most at three in the morning. She handles this by moving the graduates from a scene, to a story, to a statistic, and finally to a direct charge, and at each step she narrows what "attention" means until it is no longer a feeling but a habit they can perform. Most importantly, she concedes the exhaustion waiting for them so she can move the real danger somewhere they did not expect, from fatigue to certainty.

Quenneville opens with a sound instead of advice. The monitors "tick," the ice machine "groans," and a call light blinks "like a slow pulse." For an audience that has only done clinicals, this puts them on the floor before she asks anything of them, and the simile is telling, because even the background noise is given a heartbeat. Then she splits it: "Most of that noise means nothing. Some of it means everything." Those two short sentences set up the problem the whole speech tries to solve, which is how to tell the difference. Only after that does she define her term, calling attention "a practice, like scrubbing in." This comparison is chosen for nurses specifically. Scrubbing in is something they have done hundreds of times no matter their mood, so she borrows a habit they already respect and attaches attention to it.

The story of the man in room 412 then shows what this practice looks like. Quenneville uses flat, repeated sentences, "His vitals were fine. His chart was fine," that sound like the reassuring data a tired nurse would accept. The repetition makes the twist hit harder: the only warning sign was a request to see the sky. She also admits she "nearly told him there was nothing out there but a parking lot," which matters because she isn't posing as a hero with perfect instincts. She was a third-year nurse, not far from where the graduates are now. Her conclusion, "I did not save him with a skill. I saved him by hearing a sentence," answers her own second paragraph: skills are what they learned in school, but hearing is what she is asking for now.

She knows the graduates will push back, so she lists their objections for them. The "fourteen clicks to record a glass of water" is specific enough to be funny, and it shows she hasn't forgotten what the job is like. Because she promises "I will not insult you by pretending otherwise," her rebuttal lands harder: the nurses who miss things "decided, somewhere along the way, that they already knew what they would find." The line "Fatigue takes your legs; certainty takes your eyes" makes this memorable, but it is also a little uncomfortable for people who were just tested on knowing the answers. The confidence school rewarded is the "thief." Her hospital data backs this up, with forty-four of seventy-one rapid-response calls coming from a nurse who noticed "something was off," and repeating "Forty-four" alone forces the audience to sit with it. Still, she adds that machines "are good at what they measure." She is not telling them to ignore monitors, which would sound reckless with faculty in the room; she is telling them their job starts where the measuring stops.

By the last paragraph she has earned the right to give orders, and the tone shifts to imperatives: "stand still for three seconds," "Ask the second question." The request is concrete enough to try on a first shift. Her admission "I do not do it perfectly" keeps it from sounding like a lecture, and it actually supports her definition, since a discipline is something you never finish practicing. The ending brings back the opening scene: "The hall will be loud tonight and every night after. Listen anyway." The noise from the first paragraph hasn't gone away, and she doesn't pretend it will. Two words are the last instruction she leaves them with, which is about the right length for something to remember at three in the morning.

samples.essay:
In her commencement address, Marisol Quenneville wants the new nurses to see attention as a discipline and not a feeling, and she does this by using her own long experience to build trust and then using a story and a statistic to show that noticing people matters more than relying on machines. Because the graduates are proud of their technical skills, she has to convince them without insulting what they have learned.

She starts by describing the hospital at three in the morning, where "the monitors tick, the ice machine groans, somebody's call light blinks at the end of the hall like a slow pulse." This sensory detail puts the graduates in the place they are about to work, and the simile of the call light as a pulse makes the hospital seem alive. Then she says "Most of that noise means nothing. Some of it means everything." The short sentences set up the problem the rest of the speech is about, which is telling the difference. This is a good way to start because the graduates have never worked a night shift and she is showing them what it is like.

The most memorable part is the story of the man in room 412. Quenneville says his vitals were fine and his chart was fine, and then he asks her to open the blinds. The short sentences like "His vitals were fine. His chart was fine." sound calm and routine, which makes the moment when she asks "why" stand out. She ends with "I did not save him with a skill. I saved him by hearing a sentence." This is aimed right at the graduates, who just spent four years learning skills, and she is telling them that skill is not the whole job. The story makes her argument feel real instead of just an opinion.

Quenneville also admits the problems the graduates will face. She says they will have "six patients, sometimes eight" and be tired "in a way that has no name yet." By saying "I will not insult you by pretending otherwise" she shows she is being honest, so the audience is more likely to listen. Then she says "Fatigue takes your legs; certainty takes your eyes," which moves the danger from being busy to being sure of yourself. The metaphor of certainty as a thief makes it sound like something the graduates should be afraid of.

Next she uses the statistic that forty-four of seventy-one rapid-response calls came from nurses and not alarms. The one-word sentence "Forty-four" gives it emphasis. This proves that people notice things that machines do not, though she is careful to say she does not "disparage the machines."

At the end her tone changes to direct commands like "stand still for three seconds" and "Ask the second question." These are small, so the graduates can actually do them. She admits "I do not do it perfectly," which makes her seem human. Her last instruction, "Listen anyway," is short and tells them to keep paying attention even when the hall is loud. Overall, Quenneville uses story, honesty, and evidence to persuade the graduates that attention is something they have to choose to practice.

annotations.quote: The short sentences like "His vitals were fine. His chart was fine." sound calm and routine, which makes the moment when she asks "why" stand out.

blueprint.theme: The discipline of paying attention in nursing
blueprint.issue: Whether attention to patients is a practiced discipline that new nurses must deliberately cultivate, even when exhausted and surrounded by monitoring technology
stances: Attention is a trained discipline, not a mood, and it outperforms machines in catching what matters (speaker's stance).
Workload and fatigue make sustained attention unrealistic (anticipated objection, conceded then rebutted).

devices.function: Grounds authority in nineteen years of overnight experience and admits imperfection.
Call light like a slow pulse; attention like scrubbing in, making the abstract bodily and procedural.
Balanced opposites sharpen the central distinction between noise and signal, chart and person.
Redefines attention as a discipline to be practiced.
Keeps the graduates as the explicit audience and turns argument into instruction.
Concrete evidence that a sentence, not a monitor, saved a patient.
Repeated structures mimic routine reassurance and then enumerate the audience's coming burdens and the practice she asks for.
The patient's wish to see the sky supplies emotional stakes beyond logic.

ALTON original passage

The Six Blocks of Carrow Street
Column in a small-city newspaper, the Verrick Falls Ledger (fictional)

Last spring the council of Verrick Falls closed six blocks of Carrow Street to private cars, and the arguments have not stopped since. The owner of the hardware store says his Saturday regulars, who used to park at the curb and haul out lumber, now drive to the outlet strip on the highway instead. The woman who runs the bakery two doors down says she has never sold so many morning rolls, because people linger when nothing is idling at their backs. A nurse who finishes her shift at eleven at night asks who exactly is supposed to walk her to the garage eight blocks away. parts.prompt:
Cities of every size have begun experimenting with their downtown streets: some close a few blocks to private cars on weekends, some charge drivers to enter a central district, some remove curbside parking to widen sidewalks, and some do nothing at all. In a column for a small-city newspaper, the commentator Marisol Teague describes the quarrel that followed one such experiment:

Last spring the council of Verrick Falls closed six blocks of Carrow Street to private cars, and the arguments have not stopped since. The owner of the hardware store says his Saturday regulars, who used to park at the curb and haul out lumber, now drive to the outlet strip on the highway instead. The woman who runs the bakery two doors down says she has never sold so many morning rolls, because people linger when nothing is idling at their backs. A nurse who finishes her shift at eleven at night asks who exactly is supposed to walk her to the garage eight blocks away. A downtown is not a park, and it is not a highway either: it is a place people must be able to reach and a place people must want to stay. The quarrel is really over how much of the street each of those purposes gets to claim.

Write an essay that argues your position on the extent to which a city should limit private cars in its downtown.

Your essay should:
- Respond to the prompt with a thesis that presents a defensible position.
- Provide evidence to support your line of reasoning. Evidence may be drawn from your reading, experience, or observation, and may include (but need not be limited to) the stimulus column.
- Explain how the evidence supports your line of reasoning, and use appropriate grammar and punctuation in communicating your argument.
parts.model_answer:
Most of the fighting about car-free downtowns assumes there are only two choices: close the street or leave it alone. Marisol Teague's column about Carrow Street shows why that framing doesn't work. The hardware store owner, the baker, and the nurse are not just three opinions about cars. They are three different kinds of trips. A city should limit private cars downtown only on the blocks and during the hours when people come to stay, and it should keep car access wherever people come to fetch something heavy or have to leave after dark. How much a city restricts cars should depend on why people are on the street, not on one rule for all six blocks.

Start with the hardware store and the bakery, since they seem like opposites. The baker's customers come to linger. They buy a roll, sit down, maybe buy another, and Teague says people linger "when nothing is idling at their backs." For them the closed street is the product. The hardware customer is on an errand. Nobody lingers with a stack of two-by-fours, and nobody carries them eight blocks to a garage. So the closure costs the hardware store exactly the thing it sells, which is convenience. The fix is not to reopen the whole street. The city could put short loading bays at each end of the closed blocks, or let pickup trucks in before 9 a.m. on Saturdays. I'll admit this might not save every lumber sale. If the store is in the middle of the six blocks, a bay at the corner is still a long haul. In that case the honest answer is that some businesses don't fit a pedestrian block, and the city should either leave that one block open to slow traffic or help the store pay for delivery. Pretending the bakery's success makes up for the hardware store's loss is how the city ended up with a quarrel instead of a plan.

The nurse looks like the same complaint, but it isn't. Her problem has nothing to do with carrying anything. It's about time and safety. At eleven at night the bakery is closed and nobody is lingering, so the reason for closing the street is gone, but the closure is still pushing her eight blocks from her car. This is the easiest case to solve, because lingering happens at predictable hours. In my town, Main Street closes for the farmers market on Saturday mornings, and by one o'clock the barricades are gone and cars are parked at the curb again. Nobody fights about it, because the closure lines up with when people actually want to walk around. Carrow Street could do the same and reopen to cars at nine every night. Then the nurse isn't trading her safety for someone else's croissant.

Getting the degree wrong has consequences that reach past downtown. Teague mentions that the hardware customers now drive to "the outlet strip on the highway." If a city closes too much, it doesn't get rid of cars. It moves them, and it sorts people. Downtown ends up for people with free time and good legs, and everyone running errands, working night shifts, or unable to walk far gets sent to the highway. That's also why the right amount of restriction should change from city to city. A city with buses running late can close more, because the nurse has another way home. A small city like Verrick Falls, where the car is the only option for a lot of people, has to close less, and it has to close more carefully.

Teague says a downtown must be a place people can reach and a place people want to stay. Those two purposes don't really have to compete if the city stops treating the street as one thing. Close it when people are staying and open it when they need to reach it. The limits should be as big as the lingering and no bigger.

rubric_rows.criterion: The thesis must be about the extent of limits, not merely whether cars exist. 'Cities should limit cars somewhat' earns the point only if the essay makes clear, in the opening or the conclusion, what 'somewhat' means or on what the degree depends. A thesis may appear anywhere in the essay, including the conclusion.

Evidence counts whether drawn from the stimulus, from the writer's own town, from reading, or from reasoned hypotheticals, as long as it is specific. The writer is not required to use Teague's column at all. Commentary earns credit when it explains why a given example bears on the degree of limits a city should set, not merely on whether cars are good or bad. An essay that argues at length about climate or public health earns at most a 2 unless it connects those concerns to a decision about how much of downtown to close.

Sophistication is most often earned by essays that turn Teague's three people into a test for a principle rather than three separate complaints: for example, an essay that argues the nurse and the hardware customer are different problems (one solved by time-of-day rules, the other perhaps not solvable) and says so. Merely proposing a compromise ('close streets on weekends') does not earn the point unless the writer explains why that compromise fits the competing purposes of a downtown.

Scoring guide (ALTON practice rubric, not official College Board scoring). Each essay is worth 6 points.
Thesis (0-1): The thesis must be about the extent of limits, not merely whether cars exist. 'Cities should limit cars somewhat' earns the point only if the essay makes clear, in the opening or the conclusion, what 'somewhat' means or on what the degree depends. A thesis may appear anywhere in the essay, including the conclusion.
   - 1: A thesis that takes a defensible, arguable position on the degree to which a city should restrict private cars downtown. The position may be strong (cars should be nearly excluded; cars should be left alone), moderate, or conditional (limits should depend on time of day, size of the city, availability of transit, or the kind of business on the street). A thesis that presents a condition or a qualification still earns the point so long as it commits to something a reader could dispute.
   - 0: No thesis, or a thesis that only restates the prompt (for example, 'Cities must decide how much to limit cars downtown'), or a thesis that merely summarizes Teague's column, or a thesis that takes a position on a different question (such as whether cars are bad for the environment in general) without connecting it to how far a city should limit cars in its downtown.
Evidence and Commentary (0-4): Evidence counts whether drawn from the stimulus, from the writer's own town, from reading, or from reasoned hypotheticals, as long as it is specific. The writer is not required to use Teague's column at all. Commentary earns credit when it explains why a given example bears on the degree of limits a city should set, not merely on whether cars are good or bad. An essay that argues at length about climate or public health earns at most a 2 unless it connects those concerns to a decision about how much of downtown to close.
   - 4: Provides specific, well-chosen evidence and consistently explains how each piece advances the argument. The reasoning is organized around the writer's own distinction (for instance, the difference between people who must reach downtown and people who choose to stay there, or between delivery traffic and commuter traffic, or between cities with and without working transit), and the writer uses that distinction to decide what should and should not be limited. Counterexamples are addressed, not merely mentioned; the nurse's late-night walk, for example, is treated as a problem the writer's position must solve.
   - 3: Provides specific evidence and explains how it supports the claim, with a line of reasoning the reader can follow from paragraph to paragraph. Commentary may be uneven: one body paragraph explains carefully why a particular kind of business depends on curbside access while another simply asserts that pedestrian streets are 'more pleasant.' The writer may acknowledge an objection but treat it briefly or dismiss it rather than answer it.
   - 2: Provides some specific evidence, such as a real or plausibly described downtown the writer has visited, a family member's commute, or the baker and the hardware store from the column, but the commentary is thin or repetitive: the writer says the evidence 'proves' the point without explaining the mechanism. Typical 2-level responses also wander among unrelated points (parking, pollution, crime, noise) without a line of reasoning that orders them.
   - 1: Mostly generalities: the writer asserts that 'studies show' or 'everyone knows' that walkable downtowns thrive or that drivers abandon car-free areas, without a single specific example, scene, or observation. Or the writer lists the three people from the column (hardware store owner, baker, nurse) and says they show the issue is complicated, with no argument built from them.
   - 0: Only restates the thesis, or offers evidence that has no bearing on the question of car limits (for example, a general essay on pollution with no connection to downtown streets), or consists entirely of summary of the Teague column.
Sophistication (0-1): Sophistication is most often earned by essays that turn Teague's three people into a test for a principle rather than three separate complaints: for example, an essay that argues the nurse and the hardware customer are different problems (one solved by time-of-day rules, the other perhaps not solvable) and says so. Merely proposing a compromise ('close streets on weekends') does not earn the point unless the writer explains why that compromise fits the competing purposes of a downtown.
   - 1: The essay does one or more of the following in a sustained way, not in a single sentence: works through the real tension between access and lingering that Teague identifies and shows how the writer's position resolves it in particular cases; situates the question in a wider context (who downtown is for, how a city treats people who cannot walk far or who work odd hours, what happens to the highway strip when downtown closes); considers unintended consequences of the writer's own position and adjusts the position accordingly; or sustains a voice and style that are precise, controlled, and persuasive throughout.
   - 0: The argument is one-sided or treats the question as settled; or the essay gestures at complexity ('there are many sides to this issue') without actually working through tensions; or the prose is ornate but does not sharpen the argument.
Note: Score the essay as a whole; a strong conclusion can supply the thesis for Row A.
Note: Do not reward or penalize the writer's political stance; a well-argued case for leaving cars alone can earn a 6, and a poorly argued case for a full car ban can earn a 2.
Note: The stimulus is optional. Essays that never mention Verrick Falls are scored on exactly the same criteria.
Note: Reasoned hypotheticals ('imagine a pharmacy whose customers cannot carry a week of groceries eight blocks') count as evidence if they are concrete and the writer explains what they show.
Note: Row B scores of 3 and 4 require a visible line of reasoning; if the body paragraphs could be shuffled without loss, the ceiling is 2.
Note: An essay that argues only about a single consideration (for example, only emissions) with excellent commentary may earn a 3 on Row B but is unlikely to earn the sophistication point because it does not engage the tension the prompt names.

Sample response, middle score (4/6; Thesis 1, Evidence and commentary 3, Sophistication 0):
A city should limit private cars downtown only part of the time and only on the blocks where people mostly come to browse and eat, while keeping curbside access on the blocks where people come to carry things away. In other words, how much a city limits cars should depend on what each street is used for, not on one rule for the whole downtown.

The column about Verrick Falls shows why one rule does not work. The hardware store owner lost his Saturday customers because they used to park at the curb and load lumber, and now they drive to the outlet strip on the highway. You cannot carry lumber several blocks from a parking garage. This shows that a store that sells heavy things depends on cars, and if the city closes the street in front of it, the store loses business to the highway. The bakery owner has the opposite experience, since she sells more rolls when people can linger with nothing idling behind them. Bakeries and cafes sell a pleasant stop, so a quiet street helps them. So the closing of Carrow Street helped one business and hurt another, which means a city should look at what businesses are on a street before it closes it.

I have seen something like this in my own town. The street near my school with the coffee shops and the used bookstore has a farmers market on Sundays with the road blocked off, and it is always crowded and people seem happy. But the same weekend nobody would want the pharmacy two streets over to be blocked off, because older people drive there to pick up prescriptions and they cannot walk far. A closing that works for a market would not work for a pharmacy.

The nurse in the column is a harder problem. She gets off at eleven at night and has to walk eight blocks to the garage. I think the answer is time of day. The street can be closed during the day and on weekends when it is busy, and opened to cars at night so she can park close and feel safe. This costs the city something, because the street is less of a park at night, but there are few people lingering at that hour anyway, so the loss is small. Nobody is hurt much by letting cars back in at night, while the nurse could be hurt a lot.

Some people will say that any cars at all ruin a walkable downtown. But a downtown that nobody can reach is not walkable either, it is just empty. The best position is a middle one, with closures on the blocks and hours when lingering matters most, and cars allowed where people have to reach something. Earns the thesis point.
   - "You cannot carry lumber several blocks from a parking garage." - Uses the hardware store from the column and gives a real mechanism (heavy goods need curb access), and the point is stated rather than developed.
   - "So the closing of Carrow Street helped one business and hurt another, which means a city should look at what businesses are on a street before it closes it." - Links the two column examples back to the thesis, giving a followable line of reasoning, though the point is fairly general.
   - "A closing that works for a market would not work for a pharmacy." - Personal example is specific enough to count, but the pharmacy is described briefly and the commentary is thin and repeats the earlier point about different businesses.
   - "I think the answer is time of day." - Treats the nurse as a problem the position must solve, which is good, but the solution is stated simply and the claim that few people linger at night is asserted without support.

Cities have to decide how much to limit cars downtown and there are good points on both sides. In my opinion a city should limit cars but not too much, because downtowns need both cars and people walking.

In the column, Verrick Falls closed six blocks of Carrow Street and now people are arguing. The hardware store owner says his customers go to the highway now. The bakery lady says she sells more rolls. And the nurse is worried about walking to the garage at night. This shows that the issue is complicated because different people want different things. Some businesses like the closing and some do not.

I think that closing streets is good because people like to walk around. When there are no cars it is quieter and cleaner and people stay longer. Also it is safer for kids. A lot of cities have done this and it works for them. Studies show that walkable downtowns do better, so cities should do it more.

However, cars are important too. Not everybody can walk far, like old people or people who work late. If a city closes everything then people will just go somewhere else, like the outlet strip. That would hurt downtown. So a city should not close all of it.

   - "A lot of cities have done this and it works for them." - No city is named and no scene is described, so this is assertion rather than evidence. Commentary is absent.
   - "This way the bakery and the hardware store can both be happy and the nurse can get to her car." - Proposes a compromise but never explains how leaving some streets open would serve each purpose, or why the hardware customer and the nurse are different problems.    - "It is a balance and each city has to find the right amount for them." - Falls back on 'it's a balance' and leaves the tension unresolved. This gestures at complexity without working through it.
