parts.prompt:
Many small towns share services such as fire protection, trash collection and school districts. Some are now asking whether public libraries should be shared the same way. In the fictional Harlow Valley, four towns are deciding whether to close their four small branch libraries and build one regional hub with longer hours, more staff and more equipment, located in the largest town. Supporters say one well-funded library serves everyone better than four underfunded ones. Opponents say a library people cannot walk to is not the same service in a new building.

Carefully read the six sources that follow, including the introductory information for each source. Then write an essay that synthesizes material from at least three of the sources and develops your position on whether a group of small towns should replace several small public libraries with one shared regional hub.

Your essay should:
- Respond to the prompt with a thesis that takes a defensible position on the question, which may be unconditional, conditional, or limited to particular circumstances.
- Select and use evidence from at least three of the provided sources to support your line of reasoning, and indicate clearly which sources you are using by citing them as Source A, Source B, and so on, or by the author's name.
- Explain how the evidence supports your reasoning; do not simply summarize or list what the sources say.
- You may use the sources to support, complicate, or argue against your own position, and you may draw on your own knowledge and experience in addition to the sources.
parts.model_answer:
When people argue about the Harlow Valley libraries, they usually talk as if the only question is money versus memory. The sources show something more uncomfortable: consolidation does not get rid of a cost, it moves it. The four towns should build the regional hub, but only if they fund Source D's shuttle and reading rooms in the same vote. Without those, the "savings" just get paid by the residents of Dreyfield and Lowen Mill in miles instead of by taxpayers in dollars.

The case for the hub is real, and Desmond Kavale makes it better than anyone because he actually ran one of the branches. His point is that the current system is already unequal. Pennick has "the only children's librarian in the valley," while Dreyfield's building "has two outlets and closes at four" (Source B). Source A backs this up: Dreyfield is open twenty hours a week, and the hub would be open sixty-six. A teenager who has to borrow a car to take an online exam in Pennick is not being served by her local branch. So opponents who picture four thriving libraries are defending something that doesn't exist.

But Kavale's best number is also misleading. He says each Dreyfield visit costs 21.50 dollars and each Pennick visit costs 7.50 dollars, and Source F charts the hub at 11.40 dollars. That looks like an obvious win until you do the math for the whole system. The four branches cost 1.9 million dollars for 177,000 visits (Source A), which comes to about 10.73 dollars a visit. That is actually cheaper than the hub. The hub lowers the total bill, but it expects 37,000 fewer visits, so its cost per visit goes up rather than down. In other words, the savings come with fewer people using the library, not with more efficient service.

Who are those missing people? Source E answers that. In Dreyfield, 33 percent of residents visit their branch monthly, but only 14 percent expect to visit the hub that often, and 18 percent of households there have no car. Meanwhile Pennick's number goes up, from 41 to 44. Ilse Marrow's scene at three-fifteen puts faces on these percentages: the middle schoolers, the retired men, and the woman with "no computer and no car" who fills out forms on the one public computer (Source C). Kavale and Marrow aren't really disagreeing about facts. Kavale measures cost per visit, and Marrow measures who can get in the door. Divide dollars by visits and the number always looks better once the hardest people to serve stop showing up.

This is why Source D's conditions are not a watered-down compromise but the actual plan. The shuttle (95,000 dollars) and reading rooms (85,000 dollars) shrink the savings from 300,000 to 120,000, but they keep a public computer and a children's shelf within walking distance of Marrow's kids while also giving them a ride to a homework center their town could never afford. Marrow is right that "a schedule is a reason not to go," which is why the reading room matters more than the shuttle. It keeps the walk-in version of the library alive. Someone could say this is just a smaller copy of the four-branch system. It isn't, though, because a twenty-hour room in a town hall doesn't need its own roof and furnace, and those are exactly the costs Kavale blames.

The review matters too, because so much of the case rests on guesses. The 140,000 visits is a projection, and "expect to visit" in Source E records what people wrote on a survey, not what they will do. A plan built on predictions should come with a promise to check them, and Source D's automatic extension makes that promise binding instead of hopeful.

The grant deadline makes it tempting to vote yes and work out the details later. The valley should vote yes, but only on the version where the details are paid for up front. Otherwise the towns with the fewest alternatives end up paying for a library they mostly can't reach.

rubric_rows.criterion: A conditional position counts as defensible only if it names the condition. 'Towns should consolidate only if they fund a way for people without cars to reach the hub' earns the point; 'Towns should consolidate if it makes sense for them' does not. A thesis that picks a stance but mislabels it (calling Source D an opponent, for instance) still earns the point; source accuracy is scored in Row B.

Sources A, E and F are informational and can support any stance; using them does not by itself show synthesis unless the essay explains what the number means for its argument. Counting the number of sources cited is not enough for 3 or 4: an essay that cites five sources in one sentence each with no commentary stays at 2. Correct arithmetic drawn from the sources (for example, that the current system's overall cost per visit, 1.9 million dollars over 177,000 visits, is actually lower than the hub's projected 11.40) counts as strong evidence use. Misreading a source in a way that reverses its meaning (claiming Source D opposes the hub outright, or that Source E shows Dreyfield residents rarely use their branch) caps the row at 2 unless the misreading is minor and isolated.

A strong candidate for this point is an essay that identifies that consolidation shifts who bears the cost (from taxpayers in dollars to outlying residents in distance) and argues from that insight. Another is an essay that uses Source D's conditions to test whether a 'both' solution is really a compromise or simply a smaller version of the status quo. Vocabulary alone, a vivid opening, or a closing call to 'remember what libraries are for' does not earn the point.

Scoring guide (ALTON practice rubric, not official College Board scoring). Each essay is worth 6 points.
Thesis (0-1): A conditional position counts as defensible only if it names the condition. 'Towns should consolidate only if they fund a way for people without cars to reach the hub' earns the point; 'Towns should consolidate if it makes sense for them' does not. A thesis that picks a stance but mislabels it (calling Source D an opponent, for instance) still earns the point; source accuracy is scored in Row B.
   - 1: A thesis that takes a defensible position on whether small towns should replace several small libraries with one regional hub. The position may be a flat yes or no, a conditional yes (only with transit and local reading rooms, for example), or a limited position (hub for towns within a short distance but not for distant ones). The thesis may appear anywhere in the essay and may be more than one sentence.
   - 0: No thesis, or a thesis that only restates the prompt, only summarizes what the sources say, or states that the question has two sides without choosing one. Statements like 'There are many factors a town should consider before closing libraries' earn 0.
Evidence and Commentary (0-4): Sources A, E and F are informational and can support any stance; using them does not by itself show synthesis unless the essay explains what the number means for its argument. Counting the number of sources cited is not enough for 3 or 4: an essay that cites five sources in one sentence each with no commentary stays at 2. Correct arithmetic drawn from the sources (for example, that the current system's overall cost per visit, 1.9 million dollars over 177,000 visits, is actually lower than the hub's projected 11.40) counts as strong evidence use. Misreading a source in a way that reverses its meaning (claiming Source D opposes the hub outright, or that Source E shows Dreyfield residents rarely use their branch) caps the row at 2 unless the misreading is minor and isolated.
   - 4: Uses specific, well-chosen evidence from at least three sources, consistently explains how each piece supports the line of reasoning, and builds the paragraphs into a developed argument rather than a list. The essay engages with evidence that complicates its position (for example, a pro-hub essay that confronts the survey drop-off in Source E, or an anti-hub essay that confronts the hours and staffing gap in Sources A and B) and explains why its position still holds.
   - 3: Uses specific evidence from at least three sources to support a line of reasoning, and explains for most of that evidence how it supports the claim. The essay usually points to a particular figure, example or quotation (the 14 percent expected hub use in Dreyfield, the 21.50 dollar cost per visit, Marrow's three-fifteen scene) and says what it shows. Some commentary may still be generic or some evidence may be dropped in without explanation.
   - 2: Uses evidence from at least three sources and connects at least some of it to the thesis, but the reasoning is thin or uneven: the essay may lean on one source and mention the others briefly, make general claims ('distance is a big problem') without pointing to the specific figures or examples that show it, or leave the reader to infer why a cited fact matters.
   - 1: Uses evidence from at least two sources but mostly summarizes them in turn ('Source A says... Source B says...') with little or no explanation of how the evidence supports a position. Commentary, where present, repeats the evidence in other words.
   - 0: Restates the thesis, offers no evidence from the sources, or uses evidence from fewer than two sources with no connection to any claim.
Sophistication (0-1): A strong candidate for this point is an essay that identifies that consolidation shifts who bears the cost (from taxpayers in dollars to outlying residents in distance) and argues from that insight. Another is an essay that uses Source D's conditions to test whether a 'both' solution is really a compromise or simply a smaller version of the status quo. Vocabulary alone, a vivid opening, or a closing call to 'remember what libraries are for' does not earn the point.
   - 1: The essay does at least one of the following in a sustained way, not in a single sentence: explains why the tension exists (for example, that per-visit cost and per-person access measure different things, so Sources B and C are not actually disagreeing about facts); situates the argument in a wider context, such as what a public institution owes to the residents least able to travel; examines the limits of the evidence, such as noting that the hub visit projection is only a projection and the 'expect to visit' survey column records intention rather than behavior; or writes with a controlled, precise style that makes the reasoning clearer.
   - 0: The argument is straightforward and does not complicate its own claims, treats the issue as a simple contest between savings and sentiment, or relies on sweeping statements and ornamental prose instead of precise thought. Merely mentioning 'the other side' before dismissing it does not earn the point.
Note: Score the three rows independently; an essay can earn Row C without earning a 4 in Row B, and vice versa.
Note: Essays that cite the sources by author name (Kavale, Marrow) instead of letter are acceptable.
Note: An essay that uses only two sources cannot score above 1 in Row B regardless of quality.
Note: Numbers in the sources are consistent with one another; an essay that notices and uses a relationship between two sources (Source B's cost figures with Source F, Source C's percentages with Source E) is doing synthesis and should be credited for it.
Note: Do not penalize an essay for taking a position the grader finds unpersuasive; penalize only unsupported or self-contradicting reasoning.
Note: Personal experience with a local library counts as evidence only when it is tied to the argument; it does not substitute for the three-source minimum.

   - "The four towns should build the regional hub, but only if they fund Source D's shuttle and reading rooms in the same vote." - Earns the point. This is a conditional thesis that names its condition (funded transit and local reading rooms, approved at the same time as construction), so it's defensible and specific, not a vague 'if it makes sense.'
   - "the "savings" just get paid by the residents of Dreyfield and Lowen Mill in miles instead of by taxpayers in dollars" - Sets up the line of reasoning the rest of the essay follows: the cost doesn't disappear, it moves from taxpayers to outlying residents.    - ""expect to visit" in Source E records what people wrote on a survey, not what they will do" - Looks at the limits of the evidence (intention vs. behavior, a projection vs. actual numbers) and uses that to argue the review must be binding. Together with the cost-shift framing that runs through the essay, this makes the sophistication sustained rather than a one-sentence gesture.
   - "Otherwise the towns with the fewest alternatives end up paying for a library they mostly can't reach." - The conclusion goes back to the cost-shift insight instead of a generic 'remember what libraries are for' ending. The essay argues from that insight from start to finish.

Sample response, middle score (5/6; Thesis 1, Evidence and commentary 4, Sophistication 0):
The four towns of Harlow Valley should build the regional hub, but only if they also pay for a shuttle and keep small reading rooms open in the towns that lose their branches. Without those two things the hub would help Pennick and leave the other towns worse off than they are now.

The best argument for the hub is the one Desmond Kavale makes in Source B. He points out that the four branches are already unequal, since Pennick has the new books, the evening hours and the only children's librarian. Source F backs him up with numbers, because a visit to the Dreyfield branch costs 21.50 dollars and a visit to Pennick costs 7.50. The hub is projected to cost 11.40 per visit, which is a lot less than Dreyfield or Lowen Mill. Kavale also says that closing the branches would free up about 300,000 dollars a year for specialists. This shows that keeping four small buildings open means paying for roofs and furnaces instead of for staff and services, so the hub would be a better use of money for the valley.

However, cost per visit does not tell the whole story. If you take the whole system, 1.9 million dollars divided by 177,000 visits is about 10.70 per visit, which is actually less than the hub's projected 11.40. So the hub is not clearly cheaper per visit, and its savings come mostly from having fewer buildings. More important, the people who would lose the most are the ones with the fewest options. Source E shows that only 14 percent of Dreyfield residents expect to use the hub monthly, while 33 percent use their branch that often now, and 18 percent of Dreyfield households have no car. Ilse Marrow in Source C puts a face on those numbers with the woman from the apartments who uses the one public computer because she has no car. Marrow says a shuttle is "a schedule, and a schedule is a reason not to go," and that is a fair point, since Dreyfield is fourteen miles from the hub according to Source A.

That is why I think Source D has the right answer. The Office of Shared Services does not reject the hub, it says the hub can be recommended with three funded conditions, a shuttle, staffed reading rooms in Dreyfield and Lowen Mill, and a review after three years. These conditions cut the savings from 300,000 to about 120,000 dollars, but that is the price of making the hub serve everyone and not just Pennick. Marrow is right that a shuttle is not the same as a walk, but the reading rooms give people a place in town, which answers her concern better than a shuttle alone could.

In the end, the question is not only about money. Consolidation saves the taxpayers money, but it moves the cost onto people who have to travel, and that is only fair if the towns pay to reduce that burden. The hub with the conditions is worth building, and the hub without them is not.
   - "should build the regional hub, but only if they also pay for a shuttle and keep small reading rooms open in the towns that lose their branches" - Clear conditional thesis that names its conditions (shuttle and local reading rooms), so it earns the thesis point.
   - "a visit to the Dreyfield branch costs 21.50 dollars and a visit to Pennick costs 7.50" - Specific figures from Sources B and F, tied to the claim that small branches are inefficient. This is good evidence, though the commentary after it is fairly general.
   - "1.9 million dollars divided by 177,000 visits is about 10.70 per visit, which is actually less than the hub's projected 11.40" - Correct arithmetic combining Sources A and F, and it complicates the pro-hub case. The rubric names this as strong evidence use.
   - "only 14 percent of Dreyfield residents expect to use the hub monthly, while 33 percent use their branch that often now" - Uses Source E and the Marrow figures accurately to show the drop-off in Dreyfield. It supports the thesis, but the essay does not look at whether 'expect' is only an intention.
   - "the woman from the apartments who uses the one public computer because she has no car" - Connects Marrow's example to the Source E car-ownership figure, but the explanation is brief and a little repetitive.
   - "Consolidation saves the taxpayers money, but it moves the cost onto people who have to travel" - Names the shift of cost from taxpayers to outlying residents. It appears only in the conclusion and is not developed through the essay, so it is not sustained enough for the sophistication point.

Sample response, low score (2/6; Thesis 0, Evidence and commentary 2, Sophistication 0):
Libraries are an important part of any town and the people of Harlow Valley have a hard choice to make. There are good points on both sides of whether to build one regional hub or keep the four small libraries. In my opinion the towns should think carefully about what is best for everyone before they decide.

Source B says that the old system is not working very well. The writer ran the Oskar Bend branch for nineteen years and says that Dreyfield's building has only two outlets and closes at four. He also says it costs 21.50 dollars per visit in Dreyfield and only 7.50 in Pennick. This shows that the small libraries are expensive and the hub would save money. Source F also shows the costs, with the hub at 11.40 which is in the middle.

On the other hand Source C is about Dreyfield and it describes kids coming in at three-fifteen and a woman who has no car. The writer says a shuttle is a schedule and a schedule is a reason not to go. This is a good point because lots of people would not be able to get to the hub. Source E has a table that shows the percent of people who would use the hub is lower in Dreyfield, 14 percent, than in Pennick. So distance is a big problem for the hub.

Source D is a memo that says the hub can be recommended but only with conditions like a shuttle and reading rooms. This is a kind of middle option and it costs some money but the saving is still there.

Overall both sides have a point. The hub has longer hours and more staff but people far away might lose out. The towns should look at all of this and make the best choice for the valley.
   - "In my opinion the towns should think carefully about what is best for everyone before they decide." - No defensible position and no named condition. It says the question has two sides and tells towns to 'think carefully', which the rubric scores 0.
   - "There are good points on both sides of whether to build one regional hub or keep the four small libraries." - Restates the prompt and declines to choose a side, so the thesis point is not earned.
   - "This shows that the small libraries are expensive and the hub would save money." - Cites the 21.50 and 7.50 figures but the commentary is thin. It does not notice that the current system's overall cost per visit (1.9 million over 177,000) is lower than the hub's 11.40, so the 'save money' claim is not examined.
   - "So distance is a big problem for the hub." - Uses the 14 percent figure from Source E but the conclusion is a general claim. It does not connect to Source C's 33 percent monthly use or to car-free households.
   - "This is a kind of middle option and it costs some money but the saving is still there." - Source D is summarized with no figures (95,000, 85,000, 120,000 saving) and no explanation of how its conditions test the hub plan. The paragraph is a one-sentence summary, so evidence is mostly summarized source by source.
   - "Overall both sides have a point." - The conclusion repeats the 'two sides' framing. It does not explain why the tension exists, such as cost per visit versus access per person, or who bears the cost. No sophistication.

el_frq.title: Synthesis: One Regional Library Hub or Four Town Branches?

prompt.scenario: Many small towns share services such as fire protection, trash collection and school districts. Some are now asking whether public libraries should be shared the same way. In the fictional Harlow Valley, four towns are deciding whether to close their four small branch libraries and build one regional hub with longer hours, more staff and more equipment, located in the largest town. Supporters say one well-funded library serves everyone better than four underfunded ones. Opponents say a library people cannot walk to is not the same service in a new building.
prompt.task: Carefully read the six sources that follow, including the introductory information for each source. Then write an essay that synthesizes material from at least three of the sources and develops your position on whether a group of small towns should replace several small public libraries with one shared regional hub.
requirements: Respond to the prompt with a thesis that takes a defensible position on the question, which may be unconditional, conditional, or limited to particular circumstances.

Select and use evidence from at least three of the provided sources to support your line of reasoning, and indicate clearly which sources you are using by citing them as Source A, Source B, and so on, or by the author's name.
Explain how the evidence supports your reasoning; do not simply summarize or list what the sources say.
You may use the sources to support, complicate, or argue against your own position, and you may draw on your own knowledge and experience in addition to the sources.

sources.title: Four Towns Weigh One Library
sources.body:
The Harlow Valley Council of Governments will vote in November on a plan to close the public library branches in Pennick, Oskar Bend, Lowen Mill and Dreyfield and replace them with a single regional hub on the former cannery lot in Pennick. The four branches together cost about 1.9 million dollars a year to run and recorded roughly 177,000 visits last year. Planners estimate the hub would cost 1.6 million dollars a year to operate and draw about 140,000 visits in its first full year, a figure they expect to climb once residents adjust. Construction is budgeted at 11 million dollars, with 4 million dollars coming from a state grant that lapses if the towns do not commit by spring. The hub would be open seven days and sixty-six hours a week; the current branches range from twenty hours a week in Dreyfield to forty-eight in Pennick. It would include a recording studio, a dedicated teen floor and a staffed homework center.

"We are not closing libraries, we are finally building one that can do what people keep asking us for," said council chair Ruthanne Bexley. Opponents point to distance. Dreyfield sits fourteen miles from the cannery lot, Lowen Mill nine and Oskar Bend six, and no public bus currently connects the four towns. Lowen Mill's representative, Tobias Enright, said he would not support the plan without "a written, funded answer for the people who walk to the library today." A council survey of 1,240 residents found that willingness to use the hub was highest in Pennick and fell steadily with distance.

sources.title: Nostalgia Is Not a Library Budget
sources.attribution: Desmond Kavale, retired branch director, The Harlow Valley Courier, 2025
sources.body:
I ran the Oskar Bend branch for nineteen years, and I loved it, so understand that I say this with no pleasure: the four-branch system is already a hub-and-nothing system. Pennick has the new books, the evening hours and the only children's librarian in the valley. The other three branches have what Pennick had eight years ago. When a Dreyfield teenager needs a quiet place to take an online exam, she borrows a car and drives to Pennick, because Dreyfield's building has two outlets and closes at four. We have been asking small towns to be loyal to buildings that cannot serve them.

Look at what it costs to open the doors. Every visit to Dreyfield costs the taxpayers 21.50 dollars; every visit to Pennick costs 7.50. That gap is not because Dreyfield's staff are careless. It is because a roof, a furnace, a security system and a desk clerk cost the same whether sixteen thousand people walk in or ninety-six thousand. Consolidating would free roughly 300,000 dollars a year, enough to hire three full-time specialists instead of four part-time generalists who rotate between buildings.

Yes, distance matters. But the honest comparison is not between a hub and four thriving branches. It is between a hub and four branches that are quietly rationing hours, materials and staff, and will ration more every year the furnaces age. A valley of eighteen thousand people can support one excellent library. It is proving, year by year, that it cannot support four adequate ones.

sources.title: What Walks In at Three-Fifteen
sources.body:
At three-fifteen the Dreyfield library fills the way a bus does. Eleven or twelve kids from the middle school come in with their backpacks half unzipped, and Mrs. Pell, who has worked the desk since before some of their parents were born, does not look up from her stamping until she has counted them. Then come the two retired men who read the paper on the bench by the window, and after them the woman from the apartments across the road who uses the one public computer to fill out her forms, because she has no computer and no car.

I have asked the council what these people are supposed to do on the day the doors close. I am told there may be a shuttle. A shuttle is a schedule, and a schedule is a reason not to go. A library you can walk to at three-fifteen is a different thing from a library you can be driven to on Saturdays.

The hub will be beautiful. I have seen the drawings, the teen floor and the recording studio, and I do not doubt that somebody in Pennick will use them. But the council survey put it plainly: only fourteen in a hundred Dreyfield residents expect to visit the hub as often as monthly. Thirty-three in a hundred visit our branch that often now. You cannot call that a service improvement. You can call it a service relocated to people who already have one. If the valley has 300,000 dollars a year to find, let it find it somewhere that does not take the only public room in this town.

sources.title: Memorandum: Service Conditions for a Regional Library Hub
sources.attribution: Office of Shared Services, Harlow Valley Council of Governments, 2025
sources.body:
This office was asked whether the proposed hub can be recommended as presented. Our answer is that it can be recommended only with three conditions attached, each funded in the same resolution that approves construction.

First, a fixed-route shuttle linking Dreyfield, Lowen Mill and Oskar Bend to the hub on at least four days a week, including one weekend day, at an estimated 95,000 dollars a year. Second, a staffed reading room of no fewer than twenty hours a week in Dreyfield and in Lowen Mill, housed in existing municipal buildings, with a public computer, holds pickup and a children's shelf, at an estimated 85,000 dollars a year for both. Third, a review after three years in which the hub's visit count is compared against the 140,000 projection, with the shuttle and reading rooms extended automatically if use from the outlying towns has not recovered to current levels.

These conditions reduce the projected annual saving from about 300,000 dollars to about 120,000 dollars. We consider that reduction the price of a plan that does not simply move service from the towns with the fewest alternatives to the town with the most. Without the conditions, the survey data suggest the hub would be used mainly by Pennick residents, and the valley would have spent 11 million dollars to serve roughly the people the Pennick branch already serves. With them, the hub becomes a genuine upgrade for every town rather than a consolidation that wears the name of one.

rows.name: Thesis

descriptors.0: No thesis, or a thesis that only restates the prompt, only summarizes what the sources say, or states that the question has two sides without choosing one. Statements like 'There are many factors a town should consider before closing libraries' earn 0.
descriptors.1: A thesis that takes a defensible position on whether small towns should replace several small libraries with one regional hub. The position may be a flat yes or no, a conditional yes (only with transit and local reading rooms, for example), or a limited position (hub for towns within a short distance but not for distant ones). The thesis may appear anywhere in the essay and may be more than one sentence.

rows.task_specific: A conditional position counts as defensible only if it names the condition. 'Towns should consolidate only if they fund a way for people without cars to reach the hub' earns the point; 'Towns should consolidate if it makes sense for them' does not. A thesis that picks a stance but mislabels it (calling Source D an opponent, for instance) still earns the point; source accuracy is scored in Row B.

rows.name: Evidence and Commentary

descriptors.0: Restates the thesis, offers no evidence from the sources, or uses evidence from fewer than two sources with no connection to any claim.
descriptors.1: Uses evidence from at least two sources but mostly summarizes them in turn ('Source A says... Source B says...') with little or no explanation of how the evidence supports a position. Commentary, where present, repeats the evidence in other words.
descriptors.2: Uses evidence from at least three sources and connects at least some of it to the thesis, but the reasoning is thin or uneven: the essay may lean on one source and mention the others briefly, make general claims ('distance is a big problem') without pointing to the specific figures or examples that show it, or leave the reader to infer why a cited fact matters.
descriptors.3: Uses specific evidence from at least three sources to support a line of reasoning, and explains for most of that evidence how it supports the claim. The essay usually points to a particular figure, example or quotation (the 14 percent expected hub use in Dreyfield, the 21.50 dollar cost per visit, Marrow's three-fifteen scene) and says what it shows. Some commentary may still be generic or some evidence may be dropped in without explanation.
descriptors.4: Uses specific, well-chosen evidence from at least three sources, consistently explains how each piece supports the line of reasoning, and builds the paragraphs into a developed argument rather than a list. The essay engages with evidence that complicates its position (for example, a pro-hub essay that confronts the survey drop-off in Source E, or an anti-hub essay that confronts the hours and staffing gap in Sources A and B) and explains why its position still holds.

rows.task_specific: Sources A, E and F are informational and can support any stance; using them does not by itself show synthesis unless the essay explains what the number means for its argument. Counting the number of sources cited is not enough for 3 or 4: an essay that cites five sources in one sentence each with no commentary stays at 2. Correct arithmetic drawn from the sources (for example, that the current system's overall cost per visit, 1.9 million dollars over 177,000 visits, is actually lower than the hub's projected 11.40) counts as strong evidence use. Misreading a source in a way that reverses its meaning (claiming Source D opposes the hub outright, or that Source E shows Dreyfield residents rarely use their branch) caps the row at 2 unless the misreading is minor and isolated.

rows.name: Sophistication

descriptors.0: The argument is straightforward and does not complicate its own claims, treats the issue as a simple contest between savings and sentiment, or relies on sweeping statements and ornamental prose instead of precise thought. Merely mentioning 'the other side' before dismissing it does not earn the point.
descriptors.1: The essay does at least one of the following in a sustained way, not in a single sentence: explains why the tension exists (for example, that per-visit cost and per-person access measure different things, so Sources B and C are not actually disagreeing about facts); situates the argument in a wider context, such as what a public institution owes to the residents least able to travel; examines the limits of the evidence, such as noting that the hub visit projection is only a projection and the 'expect to visit' survey column records intention rather than behavior; or writes with a controlled, precise style that makes the reasoning clearer.

rows.task_specific: A strong candidate for this point is an essay that identifies that consolidation shifts who bears the cost (from taxpayers in dollars to outlying residents in distance) and argues from that insight. Another is an essay that uses Source D's conditions to test whether a 'both' solution is really a compromise or simply a smaller version of the status quo. Vocabulary alone, a vivid opening, or a closing call to 'remember what libraries are for' does not earn the point.

scoring_notes: Score the three rows independently; an essay can earn Row C without earning a 4 in Row B, and vice versa.
Essays that cite the sources by author name (Kavale, Marrow) instead of letter are acceptable.
An essay that uses only two sources cannot score above 1 in Row B regardless of quality.

Numbers in the sources are consistent with one another; an essay that notices and uses a relationship between two sources (Source B's cost figures with Source F, Source C's percentages with Source E) is doing synthesis and should be credited for it.
Do not penalize an essay for taking a position the grader finds unpersuasive; penalize only unsupported or self-contradicting reasoning.
Personal experience with a local library counts as evidence only when it is tied to the argument; it does not substitute for the three-source minimum.

common_pitfalls: Summarizing each source in turn without connecting the summaries to a claim.
Treating the issue as money versus feelings, when Sources E and F show that both sides have numbers and the dispute is about which numbers matter.
Misreading Source D as opposition; it supports the hub under conditions, which makes it the most useful source for a middle position.
Citing the 300,000 dollar saving without noticing that Source D shows it falls to 120,000 once access conditions are funded.

Using the cost-per-visit chart to claim the hub is cheaper per visit than the current system; the hub's projected 11.40 is lower than three branches but higher than Pennick and higher than the system's combined average.
Reading the survey's 'expect to visit the hub' column as a measure of what residents will actually do rather than what they predict.
Quoting Marrow's scene at length as decoration without explaining what it demonstrates about who uses a walkable branch.
Writing a thesis that lists considerations rather than taking a position.
Ignoring the state grant deadline in Source A, which is the reason the choice cannot simply be postponed, and so missing a chance to address urgency.

samples.essay:
When people argue about the Harlow Valley libraries, they usually talk as if the only question is money versus memory. The sources show something more uncomfortable: consolidation does not get rid of a cost, it moves it. The four towns should build the regional hub, but only if they fund Source D's shuttle and reading rooms in the same vote. Without those, the "savings" just get paid by the residents of Dreyfield and Lowen Mill in miles instead of by taxpayers in dollars.

The case for the hub is real, and Desmond Kavale makes it better than anyone because he actually ran one of the branches. His point is that the current system is already unequal. Pennick has "the only children's librarian in the valley," while Dreyfield's building "has two outlets and closes at four" (Source B). Source A backs this up: Dreyfield is open twenty hours a week, and the hub would be open sixty-six. A teenager who has to borrow a car to take an online exam in Pennick is not being served by her local branch. So opponents who picture four thriving libraries are defending something that doesn't exist.

But Kavale's best number is also misleading. He says each Dreyfield visit costs 21.50 dollars and each Pennick visit costs 7.50 dollars, and Source F charts the hub at 11.40 dollars. That looks like an obvious win until you do the math for the whole system. The four branches cost 1.9 million dollars for 177,000 visits (Source A), which comes to about 10.73 dollars a visit. That is actually cheaper than the hub. The hub lowers the total bill, but it expects 37,000 fewer visits, so its cost per visit goes up rather than down. In other words, the savings come with fewer people using the library, not with more efficient service.

Who are those missing people? Source E answers that. In Dreyfield, 33 percent of residents visit their branch monthly, but only 14 percent expect to visit the hub that often, and 18 percent of households there have no car. Meanwhile Pennick's number goes up, from 41 to 44. Ilse Marrow's scene at three-fifteen puts faces on these percentages: the middle schoolers, the retired men, and the woman with "no computer and no car" who fills out forms on the one public computer (Source C). Kavale and Marrow aren't really disagreeing about facts. Kavale measures cost per visit, and Marrow measures who can get in the door. Divide dollars by visits and the number always looks better once the hardest people to serve stop showing up.

This is why Source D's conditions are not a watered-down compromise but the actual plan. The shuttle (95,000 dollars) and reading rooms (85,000 dollars) shrink the savings from 300,000 to 120,000, but they keep a public computer and a children's shelf within walking distance of Marrow's kids while also giving them a ride to a homework center their town could never afford. Marrow is right that "a schedule is a reason not to go," which is why the reading room matters more than the shuttle. It keeps the walk-in version of the library alive. Someone could say this is just a smaller copy of the four-branch system. It isn't, though, because a twenty-hour room in a town hall doesn't need its own roof and furnace, and those are exactly the costs Kavale blames.

The review matters too, because so much of the case rests on guesses. The 140,000 visits is a projection, and "expect to visit" in Source E records what people wrote on a survey, not what they will do. A plan built on predictions should come with a promise to check them, and Source D's automatic extension makes that promise binding instead of hopeful.

The grant deadline makes it tempting to vote yes and work out the details later. The valley should vote yes, but only on the version where the details are paid for up front. Otherwise the towns with the fewest alternatives end up paying for a library they mostly can't reach.

annotations.quote: The four towns should build the regional hub, but only if they fund Source D's shuttle and reading rooms in the same vote.
annotations.comment: Earns the point. This is a conditional thesis that names its condition (funded transit and local reading rooms, approved at the same time as construction), so it's defensible and specific, not a vague 'if it makes sense.'

annotations.quote: the "savings" just get paid by the residents of Dreyfield and Lowen Mill in miles instead of by taxpayers in dollars
annotations.comment: Sets up the line of reasoning the rest of the essay follows: the cost doesn't disappear, it moves from taxpayers to outlying residents. Each body paragraph tests part of this claim.

annotations.quote: So opponents who picture four thriving libraries are defending something that doesn't exist.
annotations.comment: Takes on evidence that cuts against caution about the hub (Kavale's staffing and outlets details, plus the 20 vs. 66 hours from Source A) and says what it shows instead of just listing it. Combining B and A here is synthesis.

annotations.quote: which comes to about 10.73 dollars a visit. That is actually cheaper than the hub.
annotations.comment: Correct arithmetic from Source A (1.9 million / 177,000) checked against Source F's 11.40 dollars. The rubric names this kind of evidence use as strong. The essay then explains what it means: the savings come with 37,000 fewer projected visits.

annotations.quote: In Dreyfield, 33 percent of residents visit their branch monthly, but only 14 percent expect to visit the hub that often, and 18 percent of households there have no car.
annotations.comment: Uses specific figures from Source E accurately, ties them to Marrow's three-fifteen scene in Source C, and links both back to the 'missing visits' point. This is developed reasoning rather than a list of sources.

annotations.quote: Someone could say this is just a smaller copy of the four-branch system.
annotations.comment: Brings up a real objection to its own conditional position and answers it with evidence: reading rooms avoid the fixed building costs Kavale points to in Source B. Taking on complicating evidence like this supports a 4.

annotations.quote: Kavale and Marrow aren't really disagreeing about facts. Kavale measures cost per visit, and Marrow measures who can get in the door.
annotations.comment: Explains why the tension exists: the two sources use different measures (cost per visit vs. access per person). This is one of the sophistication moves the rubric names.

annotations.quote: "expect to visit" in Source E records what people wrote on a survey, not what they will do
annotations.comment: Looks at the limits of the evidence (intention vs. behavior, a projection vs. actual numbers) and uses that to argue the review must be binding. Together with the cost-shift framing that runs through the essay, this makes the sophistication sustained rather than a one-sentence gesture.

annotations.quote: Otherwise the towns with the fewest alternatives end up paying for a library they mostly can't reach.
annotations.comment: The conclusion goes back to the cost-shift insight instead of a generic 'remember what libraries are for' ending. The essay argues from that insight from start to finish.

samples.essay:
The four towns of Harlow Valley should build the regional hub, but only if they also pay for a shuttle and keep small reading rooms open in the towns that lose their branches. Without those two things the hub would help Pennick and leave the other towns worse off than they are now.

The best argument for the hub is the one Desmond Kavale makes in Source B. He points out that the four branches are already unequal, since Pennick has the new books, the evening hours and the only children's librarian. Source F backs him up with numbers, because a visit to the Dreyfield branch costs 21.50 dollars and a visit to Pennick costs 7.50. The hub is projected to cost 11.40 per visit, which is a lot less than Dreyfield or Lowen Mill. Kavale also says that closing the branches would free up about 300,000 dollars a year for specialists. This shows that keeping four small buildings open means paying for roofs and furnaces instead of for staff and services, so the hub would be a better use of money for the valley.

However, cost per visit does not tell the whole story. If you take the whole system, 1.9 million dollars divided by 177,000 visits is about 10.70 per visit, which is actually less than the hub's projected 11.40. So the hub is not clearly cheaper per visit, and its savings come mostly from having fewer buildings. More important, the people who would lose the most are the ones with the fewest options. Source E shows that only 14 percent of Dreyfield residents expect to use the hub monthly, while 33 percent use their branch that often now, and 18 percent of Dreyfield households have no car. Ilse Marrow in Source C puts a face on those numbers with the woman from the apartments who uses the one public computer because she has no car. Marrow says a shuttle is "a schedule, and a schedule is a reason not to go," and that is a fair point, since Dreyfield is fourteen miles from the hub according to Source A.

That is why I think Source D has the right answer. The Office of Shared Services does not reject the hub, it says the hub can be recommended with three funded conditions, a shuttle, staffed reading rooms in Dreyfield and Lowen Mill, and a review after three years. These conditions cut the savings from 300,000 to about 120,000 dollars, but that is the price of making the hub serve everyone and not just Pennick. Marrow is right that a shuttle is not the same as a walk, but the reading rooms give people a place in town, which answers her concern better than a shuttle alone could.

In the end, the question is not only about money. Consolidation saves the taxpayers money, but it moves the cost onto people who have to travel, and that is only fair if the towns pay to reduce that burden. The hub with the conditions is worth building, and the hub without them is not.

annotations.quote: should build the regional hub, but only if they also pay for a shuttle and keep small reading rooms open in the towns that lose their branches
annotations.comment: Clear conditional thesis that names its conditions (shuttle and local reading rooms), so it earns the thesis point.

annotations.quote: a visit to the Dreyfield branch costs 21.50 dollars and a visit to Pennick costs 7.50
annotations.comment: Specific figures from Sources B and F, tied to the claim that small branches are inefficient. This is good evidence, though the commentary after it is fairly general.

annotations.quote: 1.9 million dollars divided by 177,000 visits is about 10.70 per visit, which is actually less than the hub's projected 11.40
annotations.comment: Correct arithmetic combining Sources A and F, and it complicates the pro-hub case. The rubric names this as strong evidence use.

annotations.quote: only 14 percent of Dreyfield residents expect to use the hub monthly, while 33 percent use their branch that often now
annotations.comment: Uses Source E and the Marrow figures accurately to show the drop-off in Dreyfield. It supports the thesis, but the essay does not look at whether 'expect' is only an intention.

annotations.quote: the woman from the apartments who uses the one public computer because she has no car
annotations.comment: Connects Marrow's example to the Source E car-ownership figure, but the explanation is brief and a little repetitive.

annotations.quote: Consolidation saves the taxpayers money, but it moves the cost onto people who have to travel
annotations.comment: Names the shift of cost from taxpayers to outlying residents. It appears only in the conclusion and is not developed through the essay, so it is not sustained enough for the sophistication point.

samples.essay:
Libraries are an important part of any town and the people of Harlow Valley have a hard choice to make. There are good points on both sides of whether to build one regional hub or keep the four small libraries. In my opinion the towns should think carefully about what is best for everyone before they decide.

Source B says that the old system is not working very well. The writer ran the Oskar Bend branch for nineteen years and says that Dreyfield's building has only two outlets and closes at four. He also says it costs 21.50 dollars per visit in Dreyfield and only 7.50 in Pennick. This shows that the small libraries are expensive and the hub would save money. Source F also shows the costs, with the hub at 11.40 which is in the middle.

On the other hand Source C is about Dreyfield and it describes kids coming in at three-fifteen and a woman who has no car. The writer says a shuttle is a schedule and a schedule is a reason not to go. This is a good point because lots of people would not be able to get to the hub. Source E has a table that shows the percent of people who would use the hub is lower in Dreyfield, 14 percent, than in Pennick. So distance is a big problem for the hub.

Source D is a memo that says the hub can be recommended but only with conditions like a shuttle and reading rooms. This is a kind of middle option and it costs some money but the saving is still there.

Overall both sides have a point. The hub has longer hours and more staff but people far away might lose out. The towns should look at all of this and make the best choice for the valley.

annotations.quote: In my opinion the towns should think carefully about what is best for everyone before they decide.
annotations.comment: No defensible position and no named condition. It says the question has two sides and tells towns to 'think carefully', which the rubric scores 0.

annotations.quote: There are good points on both sides of whether to build one regional hub or keep the four small libraries.
annotations.comment: Restates the prompt and declines to choose a side, so the thesis point is not earned.

annotations.quote: This shows that the small libraries are expensive and the hub would save money.
annotations.comment: Cites the 21.50 and 7.50 figures but the commentary is thin. It does not notice that the current system's overall cost per visit (1.9 million over 177,000) is lower than the hub's 11.40, so the 'save money' claim is not examined.

annotations.quote: So distance is a big problem for the hub.
annotations.comment: Uses the 14 percent figure from Source E but the conclusion is a general claim. It does not connect to Source C's 33 percent monthly use or to car-free households.

annotations.quote: This is a kind of middle option and it costs some money but the saving is still there.
annotations.comment: Source D is summarized with no figures (95,000, 85,000, 120,000 saving) and no explanation of how its conditions test the hub plan. The paragraph is a one-sentence summary, so evidence is mostly summarized source by source.

annotations.quote: Overall both sides have a point.
annotations.comment: The conclusion repeats the 'two sides' framing. It does not explain why the tension exists, such as cost per visit versus access per person, or who bears the cost. No sophistication.

Supports consolidation; argues the small branches are already failing and one strong library serves the valley better

Conditional; recommends the hub only if a shuttle, small local reading rooms and a three-year review are funded in the same resolution

payload.title: Rhetorical Analysis: Marguerite Osgood, "A Woman Who Knows Where the Rocks Are"
payload.set_intro:
ALTON original passage
Remarks on the North Wharf Rezoning
Marguerite Osgood, retired harbor pilot, remarks delivered at a Tillet's Reach town meeting on the north wharf rezoning proposal, 2019

¶1 (1) For thirty-one years I climbed a rope ladder up the side of other people's ships. (2) My job was simple to describe and hard to do: bring the ship through the channel, past shoals that have sunk boats since before this town had a name, and lay it against the pier without breaking anything. (3) I am not a planner, a developer, or an economist. (4) I am a woman who knows where the rocks are.

¶2 (5) The proposal before you would rezone the north wharf for what the brochure calls a residential marina village. (6) I have read the brochure. (7) It is handsome. (8) The renderings show cafes with striped awnings, a boardwalk, furled sailboats, and not a single forklift, fuel barge, or crab pot. (9) That absence is the point of the drawing, and it ought to be the point of our discussion.

¶3 (10) Let me be fair to the people who drew it. (11) The fishing fleet is smaller than it was. (12) The ice house closed in 2011, the fuel dock loses money three months a year, and condominium taxes are real money for a town that cannot fix the culvert on Pell Street. (13) If I told you the working wharf is a gold mine, you would be right to laugh me out of the room. (14) It is not a gold mine. (15) It is a kitchen.

¶4 (16) A kitchen does not make money by itself, but try running a restaurant without one. (17) The diesel mechanic, the welder, the woman who patches nets behind the co-op, the boatyards, the supply store where half of you buy your winter boots: they are all here because the boats are here. (18) Take away the place where a boat can tie up, unload, refuel, and haul out, and the boats go to Carrow Point. (19) Then the mechanic goes. (20) Then the welder. (21) Then the kids who might have learned a trade from either of them go somewhere that still has trades to learn. (22) Last year the co-op landed just under four million dollars of catch across that wharf, and the harbor master counts about one hundred and forty jobs that touch it directly. (23) In a town of six thousand, that is the difference between a place that works and a place that is merely looked at.

¶5 (24) I want to say something now that is harder to put in a brochure. (25) On a February morning in 1994 the trawler Anna Belle lost her engine in the outer channel with a gale building from the northeast. (26) The men who went out after her were not the rescue crew at Harrow Light, forty minutes away, but Dale Cuttery in his lobster boat and two deckhands who had been drinking coffee at the fuel dock. (27) They were there in eleven minutes because they were already there. (28) A marina full of shrink-wrapped sailboats does not go out in a gale. (29) It cannot. (30) Nobody is aboard.

¶6 (31) So what are we really deciding? (32) Not whether Tillet's Reach will have a waterfront; it will have one either way. (33) We are deciding whether the waterfront belongs to the town or merely faces it. (34) A working harbor is loud, it smells of bait and diesel, and it will never photograph as well as a boardwalk. (35) But it answers back. (36) It sends out boats, it brings home fish, it teaches sixteen-year-olds to splice a line and read a falling tide. (37) The pretty version does none of those things; it only asks that we admire it.

¶7 (38) I have brought a great many ships safely in. (39) I would like, before I am finished, to help bring one town in too. (40) Keep the north wharf working. (41) Vote no on the rezoning, and then let us sit down and find another way to pay for the culvert.

parts.label: A
parts.prompt:
Speaker: Marguerite Osgood, a harbor pilot who retired after thirty-one years guiding ships into the port of Tillet's Reach, a fictional coastal town of about six thousand people. Audience: residents and elected council members gathered at a town meeting in 2019. Occasion: the council is about to vote on a developer's proposal to rezone the north wharf, the town's last commercial working pier, for a residential marina village of condominiums, cafes, and a recreational boat basin.

Marguerite Osgood spent thirty-one years as a harbor pilot, boarding arriving ships and guiding them through the channel into the port of Tillet's Reach. In 2019, the town council prepared to vote on a proposal to rezone the north wharf, the town's last working commercial pier, for condominiums and a recreational marina. Osgood, by then retired, spoke at the public meeting held before the vote. The passage below is the text of her remarks. Read the passage carefully. Write an essay that analyzes the rhetorical choices Osgood makes to persuade the town to keep the north wharf a working waterfront.

Your essay should:
- Respond to the prompt with a thesis that presents a defensible interpretation of the rhetorical choices Osgood makes and how they advance her purpose.
- Select and cite specific evidence from the passage to support your line of reasoning.
- Explain in your commentary how the evidence you have chosen demonstrates the way Osgood's choices work on her audience and serve her purpose.
parts.model_answer:
When Marguerite Osgood stood up at the Tillet's Reach town meeting, she was speaking to an audience that already knew the wharf was losing money. The developer's proposal had a simple pitch: handsome condos and cafes, and the tax money that comes with them. Osgood could not win by pretending those numbers away. Instead she builds her speech like one of her channel crossings, carefully and in order. First she earns trust as a practical insider who admits the wharf's weaknesses. Then she redefines the wharf from a failing business into infrastructure the town cannot function without. Finally she shifts the question from money to who is actually on the water when something goes wrong. By the end, a vote that looked like a budget decision feels like a decision about what kind of town Tillet's Reach wants to be.

Osgood opens by shrinking her own authority in a way that actually increases it. "I am not a planner, a developer, or an economist. I am a woman who knows where the rocks are." Listing what she is not lets her step out of the expert argument the council expects, and the plain image of the rocks suggests she knows dangers the planners don't. For an audience of neighbors, someone who climbed "a rope ladder" for thirty-one years is probably more trustworthy than a developer. Then, instead of mocking the brochure, she compliments it: "It is handsome." She never attacks the developers at all. She uses their own drawing as evidence, pointing out that it shows "not a single forklift, fuel barge, or crab pot." The brochure's silence becomes her strongest exhibit, because the audience can see for themselves what the plan leaves out.

The most important move comes in paragraph 3, where Osgood concedes the facts the other side would use against her. The ice house closed, the fuel dock "loses money three months a year," and the town "cannot fix the culvert on Pell Street." By saying these things first, she takes them away from her opponents and shows the council members who want the tax money that she is not just being nostalgic. That concession is what makes the kitchen metaphor work: "It is not a gold mine. It is a kitchen." Nobody judges a kitchen by whether it turns a profit by itself; they judge it by whether the restaurant can run without it. The metaphor changes the standard the wharf is measured by. She then shows the consequences as a chain: "Then the mechanic goes. Then the welder." The sentences get shorter as the town loses more, so the first losses fall like dominoes, and the longer final sentence about the kids who leave carries the damage past the shop floor. And because she already admitted the bad numbers, the good ones, "four million dollars" and "one hundred and forty jobs," sound like honest counts and not a sales pitch.

Osgood saves the Anna Belle story for after the economics, and the placement is deliberate. She even flags the shift, calling it "something now that is harder to put in a brochure." Once the council has heard that the wharf is worth money, she shows that its real value can't be counted. Dale Cuttery reached the trawler in eleven minutes "because they were already there." Then come two blunt sentences: "It cannot. Nobody is aboard." The image of empty shrink-wrapped sailboats quietly turns the debate from profit to safety, and from what the waterfront looks like to who is physically present on it. It is hard to argue for a boardwalk after that without sounding like you'd trade a rescue for a view.

Finally, Osgood returns to where she started. "I have brought a great many ships safely in" sets up her wish "to help bring one town in too." The piloting metaphor ties the ethos of her opening to her request, so she sounds less like an opponent of progress and more like a guide through a dangerous channel. Even her last line, "let us sit down and find another way to pay for the culvert," keeps the concession alive, so nobody in the room has to choose between the wharf and the culvert. Osgood persuades because she never asks the town to ignore its problems. She only asks it to see what the brochure left out.

rubric_rows.criterion: Acceptable theses identify at least one specific choice or pattern (the kitchen metaphor, the concession in paragraph 3, the Anna Belle anecdote, the shift from economic to moral framing, the piloting metaphor that frames the whole speech) and link it to the goal of defeating the rezoning. A thesis that lists devices with no claim about effect ('Osgood uses metaphor, statistics, and a story') is on the line; award the point only if the essay's thesis, wherever it appears, attaches those devices to a specific purpose; a generic purpose ('to persuade the town') does not count.

Choices that count as valid evidence include: the opening ethos and antithesis (sentences 1-4); the description of the brochure and the pointed absence (8-9); the concession and rebuttal (10-15); the kitchen metaphor and restaurant analogy (14-16); the enumeration of trades and the direct address 'half of you' (17); the cause-and-effect chain with 'Then' repetition and the two clipped sentences (19-20) before the longer sentence about the kids (21); the statistics and their scaling to a town of six thousand (22-23); the tone shift and anecdote (24-30), including the short sentences 'It cannot. Nobody is aboard.'; the rhetorical question and redefinition of the decision (31-33); the personification 'it answers back' and the parallel verbs (35-36); the closing metaphor of bringing a town in (38-39) and the conciliatory offer about the culvert (41). Essays need not use these labels; what matters is accurate description of the move and explanation of its effect. Merely noting that Osgood 'uses numbers' is weak; noting that she volunteers the unflattering numbers first (12) so the favorable ones (22) land as honest counts for more.

A strong candidate for this point notices that Osgood never attacks the developers, that she borrows the brochure's own silence (no forklifts) as her strongest exhibit, or that the Anna Belle story quietly reframes the question from money to safety and who is physically present on the water. Do not award the point for simply using the word 'juxtaposition' or for an eloquent conclusion attached to an otherwise formulaic essay.

payload.reference_text:
Scoring guide (ALTON practice rubric, not official College Board scoring). Each essay is worth 6 points.
Thesis (0-1): Acceptable theses identify at least one specific choice or pattern (the kitchen metaphor, the concession in paragraph 3, the Anna Belle anecdote, the shift from economic to moral framing, the piloting metaphor that frames the whole speech) and link it to the goal of defeating the rezoning. A thesis that lists devices with no claim about effect ('Osgood uses metaphor, statistics, and a story') is on the line; award the point only if the essay's thesis, wherever it appears, attaches those devices to a specific purpose; a generic purpose ('to persuade the town') does not count.
   - 1: A defensible claim about how Osgood's choices work toward her purpose. The claim may be modest (for example, that she establishes herself as a practical insider and then redefines the wharf as infrastructure rather than a business) but it must name a rhetorical move or strategy and connect it to persuading the town to keep the wharf working. The thesis may appear anywhere in the essay and may be more than one sentence.
   - 0: No thesis, or a thesis that only restates the prompt (for example, 'Osgood uses many rhetorical choices to persuade the town'), or a statement that merely summarizes what Osgood says about the wharf without making a claim about how she persuades. A thesis that takes a position on whether the wharf should be rezoned, rather than on Osgood's rhetoric, also earns 0.
Evidence and Commentary (0-4): Choices that count as valid evidence include: the opening ethos and antithesis (sentences 1-4); the description of the brochure and the pointed absence (8-9); the concession and rebuttal (10-15); the kitchen metaphor and restaurant analogy (14-16); the enumeration of trades and the direct address 'half of you' (17); the cause-and-effect chain with 'Then' repetition and the two clipped sentences (19-20) before the longer sentence about the kids (21); the statistics and their scaling to a town of six thousand (22-23); the tone shift and anecdote (24-30), including the short sentences 'It cannot. Nobody is aboard.'; the rhetorical question and redefinition of the decision (31-33); the personification 'it answers back' and the parallel verbs (35-36); the closing metaphor of bringing a town in (38-39) and the conciliatory offer about the culvert (41). Essays need not use these labels; what matters is accurate description of the move and explanation of its effect. Merely noting that Osgood 'uses numbers' is weak; noting that she volunteers the unflattering numbers first (12) so the favorable ones (22) land as honest counts for more.
   - 4: Specific, well-chosen evidence from across the passage supports a sustained line of reasoning. Commentary consistently explains how choices function for this audience: for example, why the concession about the ice house and fuel dock makes the later kitchen metaphor credible, why the Anna Belle story is placed after the numbers rather than before, or how the closing piloting metaphor returns to the ethos of the opening. The essay shows how choices work together rather than as a checklist.
   - 3: Specific evidence from several parts of the passage, with commentary that explains how at least two or three choices serve the purpose in ways tied to this audience and occasion. The essay has a line of reasoning, but one or more body paragraphs may slip into summary, or the analysis may be uneven (strong on the anecdote, generic on the opening ethos).
   - 2: Quotes or closely references specific moments and names the choices accurately, but commentary is thin or repetitive: it asserts that a choice 'makes the audience feel' or 'helps her argument' without explaining the mechanism. Typical 2 essays treat each device in isolation and do not connect them to the exigence (an imminent council vote on a developer's proposal).
   - 1: Mostly summary or paraphrase of Osgood's points about the wharf with little attention to how she says them. Evidence, if quoted, is general and commentary consists of labels ('this is pathos') with no explanation of effect on the town-meeting audience.
   - 0: Restates the thesis, summarizes the speech, or offers evidence that is not from the passage.
Sophistication (0-1): A strong candidate for this point notices that Osgood never attacks the developers, that she borrows the brochure's own silence (no forklifts) as her strongest exhibit, or that the Anna Belle story quietly reframes the question from money to safety and who is physically present on the water. Do not award the point for simply using the word 'juxtaposition' or for an eloquent conclusion attached to an otherwise formulaic essay.
   - 1: The essay does one or more of the following convincingly and throughout rather than in a single sentence: explains how the structure of the speech works as a whole (the movement from credibility, to concession, to economics, to the rescue story, to redefinition, to the closing ask); examines tensions in Osgood's rhetoric, such as the risk that a retired pilot's nostalgia could read as self-interest and how she heads that off by conceding the fleet's decline and ending with an offer to solve the culvert problem; situates the speech in its rhetorical situation by considering what council members and residents who favor the tax revenue would need to hear; or writes with a consistently precise and controlled prose style.
   - 0: Competent analysis that stays at the level of device plus effect, or an essay whose attempts at complexity are decorative (ornate vocabulary, sweeping claims about 'society') rather than analytical.
Note: Score holistically within each row; an essay that earns 4 in Row B will almost always also earn the thesis point, but check that the claim is about rhetoric, not about the merits of rezoning.
Note: Students may describe the choices without technical names. 'She stacks three short sentences so the loss sounds like dominoes falling' is full-credit commentary on sentences 19-21 even without the word 'repetition'.
Note: Essays that argue Osgood is wrong or right about the wharf are off task; score them only on whatever rhetorical analysis they contain.
Note: An essay built on one well-analyzed section (for example, only paragraph 5) can reach a 3 in Row B if the commentary is rich, but reaching 4 requires evidence from more than one part of the speech.
Note: Misreadings that distort the passage (for example, claiming Osgood opposes any change or that she dismisses the town's money problems) cap Row B at 2 because the commentary rests on a false account of the text.
